With Enzo Fernández’s deadline day signing for a British record-equalling £125m, Enzo Maresca can have zero complaints about a first window as Manchester City’s head coach. The No 8 follows two No 6s, in Elliot Anderson (£116m) and Ayyoub Bouaddi (£85m), and the wide players Allan Elias (£34m) and Iliman Ndiaye (£60m plus £5m) as major signings, the total spend on incomings about £457.5m. Factor in how City have generated about £281.8m in outgoings for a net spend of £175.7m, the divisions third-biggest of the window, and this sizable investment has to work - particularly the acquisition of Fernández. Jamie Jackson

A lack of money or, maybe, a reluctance to spend unless the finance was generated by transfers. Manuel Ugarte’s long-term injury (preventing his sale) and Joshua Zirkzee’s reluctance to move were factors. After selling Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães for a grand total not too far off £250m, they have signed eight – mainly young – players. Along the way the spine of a team now managed by Matthias Jaissle rather than Eddie Howe has been renewed and new cult heroes including the former Benfica right-back Amar Dedic and the former Manchester City midfielder Nico González are emerging. Receiving £116m for Elliot Anderson was proof that among the chaos in recent years, Forest have carried out some smart recruitment. After appointing Oliver Glasner, the club worked to provide for his needs, splashing out on Ousmane Diomande, while Xaver Schalger was a sensible acquisition for free, as was Daniel Muñoz at £22m. A No 9 was the priority and it required a club record £45m to acquire the long-term target Liam Delap, who fits the bill perfectly. Managing Editor, Nature Careers and Supplements

Effective networking does not come naturally to everyone. Credit: sanjeri/Getty

Networking is not “random socializing”, says Nessa Carey. It’s a professional skill that can be learnt and developed.

Carey, a UK-based entrepreneur and consultant, explains in a six-minute video why scientists often struggle with networking, drawing on her own experiences while working in industry and academia.

Both Carey and Caroline Dunne, an academic careers coach based in the United Kingdom and Australia, describe how to identify good people to chat to, ask insightful opening questions and circulate effectively in a room packed with strangers. In her six-minute video, Dunne recommends arriving early and says it is fine to leave an event before it formally ends.

The two videos formed part of a session on networking at Nature’s flagship Reframing Precision Medicine conference in London last month.

#882. Hull chases Thitikul in LPGA Tour finale and discusses phone 'detox'

Back-to-back defending champion Jeeno Thitikul shares the early lead at the CME Group Tour Championship; 2016 winner Charley Hull one back in Florida; watch day two live on Friday from 7pm on Sky Sports Mix and 8pm on Sky Sports Golf

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Charley Hull sits within a shot of the lead after a low-scoring opening round at the CME Group Tour Championship, where Lottie Woad and Nelly Korda also impressed.

A decade on from claiming her maiden LPGA Tour title at the season finale, Hull posted a six-under 66 at Tiburon Golf Club to stay in touch with a three-way tie for the lead.

Back-to-back winner Jeeno Thitkul made the ideal start to her bid for a historic three-peat by posting five consecutive birdies in a seven-under 65, lifting her joint-top of the leaderboard alongside Australia's Karis Davidson and Korea's A Lim Kim.

Hull is in a nine-strong contingent on six under that also contains Lauren Coughlin and Auston Kim, both part of Team USA's last Solheim Cup side, with Woad and European team-mate Celine Boutier both two off the early lead.

World No 1 Korda went straight to the range after finishing her opening-round 68 with four birdies in the last six holes, with only four of the 60-player field failing to break par on Thursday.

The season finale features an $11million (£8.4m) purse, with the tournament champion taking home a $4m (£3.04m) winner's cheque. Only the top 60 players in the season-long Race to the CME Globe get to tee it up in Florida.

A busy year for Hull has seen her win the Saudi Ladies International on the Ladies European Tour, finish runner-up to Nelly Korda at the US Women's Open and feature in Team Europe's Solheim Cup success, plus continue to contend on the LPGA Tour.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I'm so looking forward to some time off," Hull admitted. "I feel like it's been a very long season on and off the golf course. I have a lot of sponsors stuff that I've had to do and outings, then the golf and the Solheim Cup is always a tiring year.

"I'm really looking forward to just going home. After WTGL I'm going to go home, I'm going to buy myself a Nokia phone and for the whole month just change my sim over and just have a Nokia phone and just completely switch off from the world.

"Just an old school phone so I can't look at anything. Don't have to worry about anything. If anyone wants to get hold of me call me on that phone. Like I'm done with texting, I'm done with social media. I just want to have a whole month detox."

On whether she had done similar before, Hull added: "I've done it loads of times. I think I went four months back in 2019 without a phone.

"I done the whole of China and the whole of Asia swing without a mobile phone. I just had an iPad, and the person that I was travelling with just had my flight information and stuff on it.

"Honestly, I wish I was born 30, 40 years earlier - drives me bonkers all the technology and AI these days!"

Who will win the CME Group Tour Championship? Watch throughout the week live on Sky Sports. Live coverage continues from 7pm on Sky Sports Mix and 8pm on Sky Sports Golf. Get the latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract.

#881. Record crowds, legends - Bordeaux bid to escape amateur game

Bordeaux fans protested when the club were demoted to the sixth tier

The latest stop on Zinedine Zidane's homecoming tour was an important one for the new France head coach. When Les Bleus took on Turkey in Bordeaux on Sunday night, the ex-midfielder was returning to the city in which he spent four formative years of his playing career, between 1992 and 1996.

"I became a man in Bordeaux," Zidane fondly recalled in the build-up. France edged triumphed 2-1 with an uninspiring display, but it did not dampen the mood of the 40,000 fans inside the Stade Atlantique.

While the 1998 World Cup winner was not necessarily in familiar surroundings (the out-of-town stadium was built for Euro 2016, 20 years after his departure for Juventus), locals made every effort to make him feel at home, holding up a commemorative tifo before kick-off and chanting Zizou's name throughout.

Just a few miles up the road earlier that afternoon, Zidane's former club were playing their fifth match of the season in the sixth-tier Regional 1, in a north-western suburb of the city.

Thousands of Bordeaux fans had made the short away outing to Saint-Medard-en-Jalles' 3000-seater ground to watch their team seal a fifth win in five this season.

Girondins de Bordeaux, the six-time French champions, who were once regulars in European cups, now find themselves facing amateur opposition on a weekly basis.

Since 2022, the club has plummeted from Ligue 1 to the sixth tier through a combination of on-pitch struggles, mismanagement at all levels, and sanctions due to their financial troubles.

Listen to the latest Football Daily podcast

The club was taken over in 2021 by Gerard Lopez, who was previously in charge of Formula 1's Lotus as well as another French side, Lille.

While Bordeaux were already hamstrung by debts at that point, the situation on and off the pitch worsened under the Spanish-Luxembourgish businessman as the men's first team finished rock bottom of Ligue 1 in his first season.

A couple of seasons in Ligue 2 followed, before the club was docked down to the fourth tier in 2024. In their first National 2 season, they notably signed Andy Carroll but ultimately missed out on promotion.

The following campaign saw a repeat of that near miss, and the club was expelled from national-level football altogether this summer over their finances.

With Bordeaux left on the brink and whittled down to just eight full-time employees (down from around 250 a few years beforehand), Lopez sold up to Park Bench, a group of mainly British USA-based investors who also own Scottish side Dunfermline as well as a minority stake in Spanish second tier side Cordoba.

The supporters turned out in their numbers for the first home match of the campaign, which had been delayed amid the uncertainty over whether the club could continue running, against Stade Montois.

More than 11,000 tickets sold, a record crowd for that level of French football.

"140 years of history, we won't be stopped," read one of the banners held up by the Ultramarines fan group, who also made it a point to thank the seven first-team players who had stayed despite the club's double relegation.

The team is centred around a core of players with Ligue 1 and Ligue 2 experience. Steve Shamal, who scored a hat-trick in that 4-1 victory over Stade Montois, previously turned out for the likes of Caen and Annecy in the second tier.

"We know we should be higher up, but that certainty can also be a trap," said Shamal after the game. "We shouldn't think that it's going to be easy.

"We need to respect our opponents if we're going to put in good performances."

As the sixth tier of French football is regionalised, only the league winner in the Nouvelle Aquitaine region's top flight will earn promotion.

Their on-pitch success so far this season comes as little surprise given the gulf in quality compared to the rest of the league. Over the summer, Bordeaux notably managed to hold on to Europa League-winning full-back Almamy Toure, while former Belgian youth international striker Baptiste Guillaume also joined.

Several former players have also looked to get involved in Bordeaux's revival.

Benoit Tremoulinas, the former French international who was a part of the title-winning squad in 2008-09, notably announced that at the age of 40 he would be lacing up his boots again seven years after injury forced him to retire.

Paul Baysse, the former centre-back, is an assistant to head coach Arnaud Cormier.

Benoit Tremoulinas spent six years at Bordeaux, winning a league title and two cups, before also twice winning the Europa League with Sevilla

Perhaps the most significant endorsement the new owners could have hoped for was that of Alain Giresse, widely regarded as the club's greatest player. The Euro 1984 winner, who won three league titles while playing more than 500 times for the Marine et Blanc, was in attendance for the match against Stade Montois. He took the ceremonial kick-off before giving a full-time dressing room speech.

The new management unveiled their long-term plans for the club on Monday at Le Haillan, the city-owned training ground which includes a chateau that hosts the club's headquarters.

"We are humbled to have this responsibility," Park Bench investor Jeremy Green said.

"The club doesn't belong to Park Bench, it belongs to Bordeaux, it belongs to the 11,000 people who came to watch a Regional 1 game, to the players and to the community. We have a responsibility to rebuild this club.

"Our commitment to the community and to the players is that we will be fiscally responsible and patient.

"We're not a financial institution, we're a collection of individuals who bring with them business, sporting, analytical, and entrepreneurship skills."

Dominique Delport, the club's new president, revealed he knew Green and Twining through his wife, who studied at Oxford with them.

"We can learn from the club's golden years," the former journalist and advertising executive told BBC Sport, before adding that he would look to bring club legends to every league game.

Bordeaux won the Coupe de France as recently as 2013

While the club was sold for a symbolic euro, it did involve taking on long-standing debts which spanned transfer fees, stadium rent, and a compensation claim by former head coach Vladimir Petkovic.

Last Friday, the city's commercial court approved a request to restructure the debt as part of the club's continuation plan.

When Bordeaux were expelled from national-level football by the French FA at the start of the summer, the club used several avenues to appeal while the takeover was being finalised.

"We thought we had acquired the club in National 1 [the fourth tier]," Green and co-investor James Twining, told BBC Sport.

"Initially we walked away, but we were encouraged to come back," Green added. "We established that we were going to be able to restructure things and make it work.

"People around the club and in the local community encouraged us to try to find a way."

The six-time French champions have a long way to go before returning to the top flight.

"We're committing to a sensible financial structure, to a well-run club, and we're talking about 10 years to get this club back to Ligue 1," the new investors added.

A crucial step towards that long-term goal will be returning to the professional leagues, which would allow them to re-open the youth academy they were made to close when they dropped down.

Rebuilding the women's team, who were involved in the Champions League only a few seasons ago, is another one of the new owners' objectives.

Keeping the fans onside throughout the process will also be key, not least after the rift that opened up between groups during the previous ownership.

In any case, if the record-breaking turnout for Bordeaux's return to league action is anything to go by, their support seems unlikely to waver anytime soon.

#878. Humphries shocked by Sykes in last-leg thriller at Grand Slam of Darts

Luke Humphries is out at the last 16 stage of the Grand Slam after losing to Tom Sykes; Humphries was struggling with a trapped nerve in his shoulder; you can watch the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports until November 22

Sports Journalist @MegWellensX

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Luke Humphries suffered a last-leg 10-9 loss to debutant Tom Sykes in the second round of the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton.

It is the second big shock in the space of two days following world No 1 Luke Littler's loss to Jermaine Wattimena. Now, with the world No 2 also out, the competition is well and truly blown wide open.

Humphries looked to be struggling with a problem in his shoulder throughout the contest but managed to find some strong darts to take the contest all the way.

But Sykes, who is now ranked 72nd in the world, held on and prevailed to pick up the biggest win of his career and reach his first ever major quarter-final.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

It means Humphries will have to wait to try and clinch his second Grand Slam title following his victory back in 2023.

"I was a bit nervous, but obviously I thought the game was over when I turned around and saw Luke hit the first treble 18 there, and hit the second one and then wired it," Sykes told Sky Sports following his win.

"I was so cold on that last one. I just thought, just hit it first out, no messing about, and get into it. And I did.

"I'm just riding a wave at the minute. I'm not really bothered who I play. I'll just come back up here and we'll see what happens."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

For Sykes, a mouth-watering clash with Michael van Gerwen awaits after he came through with a remarkable contest against James Wade with a 10-8 victory.

It marks Van Gerwen's first ranking quarter-final of 2026 and he earned it in some style with a near 104 average. There was nothing separating two darting juggernauts throughout the high-quality bout, a massive 121 checkout from the Dutchman levelling the game at 7-7 before rattling off two more legs to move 9-7 ahead.

Wade did not give up and a stunning 130 checkout, his second of the match, broke Van Gerwen's throw but the three-time Grand Slam champion broke straight back and pinned D16 for the win.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"To play in these types of games was even worse. I made it incredibly difficult for myself. That's sometimes so annoying," Van Gerwen told Sky Sports.

"I couldn't hit a double after the second break and with James Wade standing behind me - it's so annoying - but it's also his class. I dealt with it the right way, and now I feel comfortable now.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Sykes made it clear he would be making the match a real contest in the first session. He averaged 107.42 in a staggering opening five legs that saw him win four with incredible ease against the in-form player in the darting world.

Although still looking uncomfortable, Humphries fought back as Sykes went slightly off the boil. That saw him pick up four of the next five legs to level the game at 5-5.

The game continued to go back and forth as Humphries found some of his top levels, but Sykes would not back down, fighting back despite some strong finishing from 'Cool Hand', a 114 finish on tops the highlight.

It then looked like it was all going to go the way of Humphries when he powered in back-to-back 11-darters to take the game to a final-leg showdown but the 'Castleford Tiger' showed why he has become a formidable player.

Humphries missed D10 to finish off a 128 checkout which allowed Sykes to have his match dart at 36. He pinned that first dart for a win to remember.

Humphries took to social media after the contest to congratulate Sykes and admitted he has been through a tough 48 hours.

Humphries said: "Well done Tom Sykes absolutely amazing performance!

"So proud of the way I played tonight with what I've had to go through with injury the last 48 hours gave it my absolute all there.

"Wish everyone all the best for the rest of the tournament."

Sykes has been on the darting circuit since 2013 when he competed on the PDC Challenge Tour and then followed that up with a year on the PDC Development Tour.

It is over the last two years that Sykes has truly flourished. He qualified for the 2025 UK Open and made it all the way to the third round.

Earlier this year he clinched his Tour card at Q-School and has since made it to the fourth round at the UK Open before picking up the win of his career with the scalp of the world No 2 on the Grand Slam stage.

The 34-year-old hails from Castleford in West Yorkshire and his nickname 'The Castleford Tiger' is an ode to the rugby league side from his hometown.

Nathan Aspinall made it through to the quarter-finals with a hard-fought 10-7 victory over Gabriel Clemens.

Aspinall apologised post-match for "writing off" the German player before the game and it was clear why, with Clemens averaging 96.55 and hitting 10 180s.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

It was a topsy-turvy game throughout the first two sessions and at the end of them, the scores were level at 5-5.

However, it was from there that Aspinall took control. From 6-5 down, he took out four legs in a row and found a massive 'Big Fish' finish for a break of throw to send the Wolverhampton crowd wild.

Clemens did manage to get one more leg on the board but in the 17th leg, Aspinall scored highly and clinched D16 for a spot in the last eight.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

He will take on Gian van Veen after he held off a fightback from Martin Schindler for a 10-7 win.

It was in the second session that the world No 3 stepped things up. Averaging over 104, he took advantage of Schindler's clear issues on the doubles to take out four of the five legs to be 7-3 ahead.

Van Veen then made that seven out of eight legs and was one leg from victory before a period of poor scoring for the third seed and a massive improvement from Schindler saw the German take out four legs to put the pressure on.

Eventually, Van Veen found back-to-back 134s and took out 93 to book the showdown with Aspinall.

#877. FA explored legal challenge to Infantino staying on

Gianni Infantino has been leading Fifa since 2016

The Football Association has considered challenging Gianni Infantino's eligibility to run for a fourth term as Fifa president, BBC Sport can reveal.

But it believes any attempt to prevent him from standing in the election in March is likely to fail.

The FA has also confirmed it is backing rival candidate Philippe Diallo.

Infantino oversaw the introduction of a three-term limit when he replaced Sepp Blatter as leader of world football's governing body.

However, Fifa's council agreed in 2022 that his first period in office from 2016 to 2019 should not count as it was the remainder of his predecessor's interrupted final term after resigning.

Earlier this month, human rights campaign group Fair Square wrote to the FA claiming that the decision is open to legal challenge and was "contrary to the spirit and purpose" of Fifa statutes.

It urged the FA to ask Fifa's governance committee to bar Infantino from the election in March because he has already served the maximum three terms.

FA chair Debbie Hewitt has now replied, telling Fair Square that the governing body "has explored the possibility of challenging Mr Infantino's eligibility to run for a further term as the Fifa president but does not consider that such a challenge would secure the outcome sought".

In correspondence seen by the BBC, Hewitt adds: "Ultimately the process followed Fifa's governance and led to an outcome where Mr Infantino's part term was disregarded for the purposes of maximum term limits.

"Having considered the process in detail, we do not believe that a challenge would succeed."

In a statement, Fair Square said: "It's understandable that the FA has no faith in Fifa's internal processes to hold Infantino accountable for serious breaches of the rules, but it's a mistake to abandon these channels, not least because it sends a signal to Infantino that he can do whatever he likes.

"We will encourage the FA to leave its options open where this matter is concerned not least because Debbie Hewitt's position on the Fifa council puts her in a very strong position to demand clear answers on why Fifa discounted Infantino's first term."

Miguel Maduro - a former head of Fifa's governance committee - has said a national association or confederation may need to challenge Infantino's eligibility at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas).

However he has also said that the ability of European football associations to do so has been made harder by Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin deciding to stand for a fourth term earlier this year. Ceferin reversed a previous insistence, in 2024, he would not seek re-election.

The FA was among a number of national associations to withdraw its support of Infantino in the wake of the crisis sparked by his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors.

European confederation Uefa has backed rival candidate Diallo, the president of the French Football Federation.

Hewitt, who became a member of Fifa's council in 2023, also told Fair Square that the FA "remains opposed to Mr Infantino's re-election and is committed to providing its full support to Philippe Diallo as our preferred candidate in the upcoming Fifa presidential election".

Last month Hewitt told BBC Sport that Infantino was not fit to lead world football unless he released documents and answered questions relating to the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan.

It has previously referred to the fact that in 2022 its council "unanimously confirmed its agreement with the view of the governance, audit & compliance committee that the period between 2016 and 2019 does not count as a term of office for the current Fifa president, who is therefore about to end his first term".

#875. Sykes ready to go 'all the way' on debut at Grand Slam after stunning Humphries

Tom Sykes came up with a thrilling 10-9 victory over Luke Humphries at the Grand Slam of Darts; It sees him through to the quarter-finals on debut; you can watch the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports until November 22

Sports Journalist @MegWellensX

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Tom Sykes pulled off the biggest win of his darting career with a 10-9 victory over Luke Humphries in the last 16 at the Grand Slam of Darts - but he does not want to stop there.

The 'Castleford Tiger', who is making his debut in Wolverhampton, put in an incredible performance against the world No 2 in which he raced away before 'Cool Hand' fought back to take the game to a last-leg decider.

Sykes scored amazingly in that winner-takes-all leg and with Humphries unable to finish off the 128 checkout, he clinched D18 to set up a quarter-final showdown with Michael van Gerwen after his 10-8 win over James Wade in the final match of the night.

Sykes is ranked 72nd in the world in what is his first year on the PDC Pro Tour but, with the way he is playing, he sees no reason why he cannot go on a real run at the Grand Slam.

"I think so. I know I have got the scoring game," Sykes said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I know I have got the scoring game to live with anyone in the world, and I have shown it tonight with the 180s and the 140s that I have been hitting.

"If the doubles go in, then I'm a dangerous player."

Humphries was suffering with a shoulder injury throughout the contest and Sykes did not realise until they were practicing and was gingerly picking up his darts.

Despite the clear pain Humphries was in, Sykes still feels he was up against the best darts player in the world playing some of the best darts in the world.

"I can't believe it, honestly. Luke didn't tell me till the end, but he said he had a bit of an injury there. I could tell, to be fair," he added.

"In the practice darts at the beginning, he was dropping his darts and he could barely bend over to pick them up.

"He still played really well and I got off to a really good start. To get 4-1 up against, in my opinion, the best player in the world at the minute, I'm absolutely buzzing with that.

"For me, he is still one of the best players in the world, even if he's injured or not. I am just buzzing to get the win over him."

Many a player would be overawed with the experiences that Sykes is now having but, as someone who enjoys the big stages, he is revelling in rubbing shoulders with the top stars of the sport.

"When I first started on the Pro Tour and I'm walking in, you see Luke Humphries, Luke Littler, Michael van Gerwen, James Wade. It is a bit daunting walking in and seeing all these guys who you've watched on TV," Sykes said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I have been in there tonight and I've been playing with Gian van Veen and with James Wade. You are like, 'what am I doing in here with these lot?'

"Now I am mixing it with these on the big stages, it is mad.

"I have always said that I am a big stage player, I like playing on big stages.

"I massively put the hard work in for the last year, and I ended up getting my Tour card last year, and now I'm reaping the rewards of it."

Our top tipster Lewis Jones, aka Jones Knows, provides his analysis and betting insight as the Premier League returns from the international break.

This 12.30pm kick-off slot has been particularly fruitful for goals backers in the game after the November international break. Perhaps it's the disrupted defensive structures or simply players taking a little longer to rediscover their rhythm. Whatever the reason, the goals tend to flow.

The last 15 fixtures played in this slot immediately after an international break have averaged a whopping 3.5 goals per game. All 15 have cleared the over 1.5 goals line, while 11 have produced three or more goals.

There's another layer to this argument, too. The Premier League is currently running below expectation in the goals department. We're seeing 2.73 goals per game despite the underlying expected goals data suggesting that figure should be closer to 2.92.

That's a sizeable gap. And one I'd expect to narrow as the season progresses such is the attacking talent on show.

Manchester City remain dangerous enough to win this comfortably if their attacking combinations click but their ability to control games without allowing opponents opportunities has been questionable.

Fulham have the attacking tools to turn this into an entertaining game and the statistical backdrop makes the 10/11 on both teams to score and over 2.5 goals with Sky Bet a very tempting proposition.

My admiration for Unai Emery is well documented. He's one of the finest coaches in the Premier League and a manager whose tactical intelligence gives Aston Villa a fighting chance against just about anyone.

But admiration doesn't pay the bills in this game. Finding value does.

And I'm not convinced Villa have done enough to justify being odds-on favourites here.

They remain a team with a few too many rough edges to be trusted at short prices, especially at Villa Park where they've failed to deliver for favourite-backers in each of their last four Premier League home games.

That's a worrying trend for anyone steaming into the home win.

Sunderland, meanwhile, are a profitable betting proposition when the market writes them off. Backing them to win with a £1 level stake in every Premier League away game since the start of last season when priced bigger than 2/1 would have returned a handsome £7.70 profit.

That tells you the market has been consistently underestimating their ability to compete on the road.

Rather than getting greedy with the away win, the Sunderland double chance at Evens with Sky Bet looks the way to play.

Bournemouth don't get nearly enough credit for just how good they are without the ball. There's a perception that they're all about high-octane pressing, attacking intent and causing chaos. But dig beneath the surface and you'll find one of the most disciplined defensive units in the Premier League.

No team has conceded fewer shots inside their own penalty area this season than Bournemouth's 59, while their expected goals against figure of just 1.13 per 90 is the third-best in the division.

And who's sitting second in that particular metric? Nottingham Forest at 1.10.

So we're dealing with two teams whose defensive foundations are among the strongest in the league. That's usually my cue to start sniffing around the unders market.

Bournemouth home matches have been a profitable hunting ground for under 2.5 goals backers since the start of last season, returning a healthy £6.56 profit to £1 level stakes. Five of their last six Premier League home games have also failed to produce three goals.

That's no coincidence. Bournemouth are far more controlled than their reputation suggests.

At Evens with Sky Bet, under 2.5 goals looks best bet of the weekend material.

There is a danger of the market pricing this one with far too much on reputation.

Chelsea are 17/20 favourites with Sky Bet, with Leeds available at 29/10 for the away win.

That's a significant gap between two sides who could produce a much tighter contest than those prices suggest.

Leeds have become an awkward opponent to shake off under Daniel Farke. They possess a granite chin, defend their penalty area with determination and are happy to make life uncomfortable for the opposition without much worry about the aesthetics of their performances. This is exactly the type of opponent that Chelsea have yet to master. See defeats to Brentford and Sunderland this season as examples.

Leeds do find it tough to score goals though, netting just four in their last seven away Premier League games. Combining them on the double chance with them to score under 1.5 goals, meaning we're covering the 0-0, 1-1 and 0-1 win looks a price worth considering at 23/10 with Sky Bet.

The managerial merry-go-round is spinning again. Crystal Palace have jumped aboard, handing Thomas Frank the keys to Selhurst Park. New hope. But a new manager doesn't necessarily mean new results.

In fact, recent evidence suggests quite the opposite for teams in trouble.

The famous 'new manager bounce' is one of football's most romanticised theories. A fresh face walks through the door, standards supposedly rise overnight and points start rolling in.

Of the last six Premier League teams sitting in the bottom eight to change manager between November and March, five actually saw their points-per-game average drop across the following five matches.

Vitor Pereira at Nottingham Forest. Igor Tudor at Tottenham. Rob Edwards at Wolves. Graham Potter at West Ham. Ivan Juric at Southampton.

It's a fascinating trend that should serve as a warning to Palace supporters expecting Frank to arrive waving a magic wand, especially with Frank having plenty to prove in that he can operate to the level expected without the comfort blanket of the Brentford structure. Spurs have won just five of last 28 Premier League home games, albeit they are searching for three wins on the spin in front of their own faithful. Things are looking up but are they a trusty steed just yet? No.

The markets still haven't quite cottoned on to what Roberto De Zerbi is cooking up either. The reputation remains one of chaos, risk-taking and goals galore. But the reality? Something very different.

Across his 17 matches in charge, Spurs games are averaging just 2.1 goals.

This isn't De Zerbi-ball of old. It's a more controlled and pragmatic version. Tottenham are prioritising defensive structure over attacking fireworks and the market seems reluctant to adjust.

We're being offered 5/4 with Sky Bet on under 2.5 goals here. That looks a lovely price considering the evidence.

Lewis Hall's performance for England in that Nations League victory over Spain was outstanding. He's made the left-back position his own for Thomas Tuchel and is now carrying himself with the swagger of an established international.

That's filtering into his Newcastle performances, too.

Hall isn't just content with doing the dirty work defensively. He's adventurous, positive and increasingly willing to get himself into shooting positions. He's registered a shot in 11 of his last 15 Newcastle starts, averaging 1.1 shots per 90 minutes - very respectable numbers for a left-back.

Hall is also the most fouled defender in the Premier League, drawing an average of 2.2 fouls per 90 across his last 12 matches in all competitions. His willingness to carry the ball into dangerous areas and take opponents on makes him a magnet for contact.

Brighton have quickly developed into one of the Premier League's most exciting outfits, playing with a level of confidence and attacking invention that makes them extremely difficult to contain.

And at the heart of it all is Pascal Gross. The man has a football brain that operates on an entirely different frequency to most mere mortals.

Only Erling Haaland and Evanilson have registered more Premier League goal involvements than Gross, who has eight to his name, four assists and four goals. There are quicker players. More explosive players. But very few who think the game quite like Gross.

The prices surrounding this influence in the goalscorer markets haven't adjusted fully with the 5/2 with Sky Bet about him scoring in a game that Brighton are heavy odds-on to win certainly offering up some value. Gross is also the designated penalty taker for this goal heavy Brighton team, too.

Anfield. Liverpool. Manchester United. Maurico Pochettino making his Premier League return. This is a fixture with enough history, pressure and emotional baggage to turn an ordinary Sunday afternoon into complete bedlam.

Pochettino has walked into a mess at United though. A team find themselves in the relegation zone at this stage of a season for the first time in 40 years. A footballing catastrophe for a club of their stature.

The defensive numbers are particularly frightening. United have shipped 30 goals in just 15 matches across all competitions this season. Only Lens (31) have conceded more among teams in Europe's major leagues.

And here's the problem for Pochettino. You can't fix that level of dysfunction with a few training sessions and a motivational team talk. Not with the same personnel, anyway.

Yet I'm not expecting an absolute goalfest. Liverpool have shown they can control matches without needing to turn them into basketball games. Pochettino's first priority surely has to be making United harder to beat, which could mean sacrificing attacking ambition to protect a defence desperately short of confidence.

That points towards a relatively controlled Liverpool victory rather than an Anfield demolition job.

At 17/10 with Sky Bet, Liverpool to win and under 3.5 goals looks the smart way to play this.

This looks a proper Monday Night Football arm wrestle. Two sides who are comfortable in their own skin, two managers who understand the value of defensive organisation and a fixture where the first goal could completely change the tactical landscape. It's classic Premier League where the margins are so fine and trying to dig out a prediction on the outright market is a tough task.

The numbers behind this particular scheduling sweet spot are rather tasty.

The last 15 Monday Night Football fixtures played immediately after an international break have averaged 3.1 goals per game. The latest instalment, Coventry's meeting with Newcastle, served up five goals for our entertainment.

Coincidence? Perhaps. But there's a theory worth exploring here.

Unlike the dreaded Saturday lunchtime slot, where managers are often scrambling to get their international players back into shape, Monday night offers an extra couple of days on the training ground. More preparation time, sharper attacking patterns and potentially more fluid football.

And when Brentford are involved at home, the goals argument gets even stronger. Their last 85 home matches have averaged exactly three goals per game. That's a substantial sample size and one that tells you plenty about the type of football we're likely to see.

Everton should have their moments, too. The market is offering Evens on both teams to score and over 2.5 goals with Sky Bet and the 2-2 correct score at 10/1 also worth a nibble.

#871. ‘When I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West’: the two lives of Bromley footballer Omar Sowunmi

Full-time defender and part-time model, the 31-year-old is happy to shine a light on both sides of his dual career

“I was walking down the street one day and someone came up to me and said: ‘I think you should be a model,’” the Bromley defender Omar Sowunmi says. He was already living out many people’s dreams as a professional footballer but was able to assume an alter ego in the world of fashion. There are few parallels between the grind of lower-league football and Milan fashion week but the 31-year-old is adept in both worlds.

Sowunmi’s dual career mixes trips to Doncaster with visits to Paris. On Saturday Bromley travel to Reading under their new manager, Karl Robinson, as they attempt to move off the bottom of League One and the centre-back is clear where his focus lies even after his chance encounter with a model agency employee expanded his horizons.

“I’d get asked to go to a job or I’d even get booked for a job and they’d be like: ‘Oh, we want you to come to Germany for three days,’” Sowunmi says. “But I had to say: ‘I can’t do it, my priority is football.’ As fun and different as [modelling] is, it’s not my main job. Football was my priority and is my priority.

“It’s wicked, the stuff I’ve done modelling. Going to Milan fashion week, being taken to Paris fashion week with brands like Christian Louboutin is a level that I never thought I would reach or be possible when I first started it. Some of the people I’ve met doing it … when I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West … just celebrities and people that I grew up listening to and I feel like without that it probably wouldn’t have happened.”

Sowunmi takes the Nobu Pilates with teacher Marsha Lindsay class twice a month in the five-star hotel of the same name in central London. He is an imposing presence at 1.98m (6ft 6in) tall and grimaces through the session as his muscles are put to the test to keep him in shape for both his professions. It helps him to battle robust strikers and appear on social media as part of modelling campaigns. “Two days ago one of my current coaches said: ‘You popped up wearing a coat on my Instagram the other day. Can you get me one?’” Sowunmi says. “But I had to explain that it doesn’t really work like that.”

Sowunmi’s career path since he left his first club, Ipswich, without making an appearance has been that of a true lower-league player, taking in spells at Yeovil, Colchester and – between two stints with Bromley – Sutton. On the catwalk, he has rubbed shoulders with some of the biggest names in the industry while promoting designer brands and plans to continue doing that once he retires from the day job. He uses social media not only to post videos and images from photoshoots but to show the reality of life as a footballer.

“The fans and everyone that watches you on Saturday or Tuesday or whatever day you’re playing, they get to see you for 90 minutes and they don’t see the full dedication that goes into being a professional footballer,” Sowunmi says. “We’re away from our families for two days [for away games]; we’ll train on the Friday then leave, maybe have a seven-hour coach journey. We’ll have stuff to do at the hotel, stretching sessions, pool sessions, nutrition. We’ll wake up and we’ll have more stuff to do and it’s that whole buildup that I kind of want to show them and give them an insight into what we do.”

Last season Sowunmi helped Bromley gain promotion to third tier for the first time. The step up has been difficult, costing the long-serving manager Andy Woodman his job. “It’s been tough, as you can tell by the league position,” Sowunmi says. “It’s a completely different league. It’s taken a lot of the players by surprise, the difference between League One and League Two, but we’re grinding, we’re working hard and I’m sure it will turn for us.”

A carefully curated moustache sits atop Sowunmi’s lip to raise money for Movember. He is speaking at a charity event on Wednesday to highlight the importance of mental health, a subject close to his heart since his best friend took his own life. “It’s something that is really deep in my heart just being a voice for people and trying to help make a difference in any way that I can,” Sowunmi says. “I was actually on an away trip and I received a call from his dad to give me the news.

“Everyone was asking me what was wrong on the bus and that I wasn’t really speaking to anyone and then I think when we got home it was a four-, five-hour journey. The manager took me to the side and got me to open up to him a little bit. Looking back that actually helped a lot, so I thought if I can help someone to speak to someone or know that it’s fine to speak to someone then I’m definitely here for it.”

#870. Anthropic IPO: four ways the AI giant wants to disrupt science

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Shares in the artificial intelligence firm Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on Thursday, in the biggest initial public offering of all time.Credit: Idrees Mohammed/AFP via Getty

Anthropic, the frontier artificial-intelligence company, has made history with the largest initial public offering (IPO) on record on 19 November. With a staggering valuation of around US$1.5 trillion, the firm, based in San Francisco, California, is now among the world’s most valuable companies — and it has major ambitions in science.

The maker of AI model Claude, Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a group who broke away from rival giant OpenAI. Its models have proven powerful in research, and Anthropic has launched its own directed science effort, focusing on areas including quantum mechanics and protein design. This year alone, it has reported mathematics breakthroughs and launched its first life sciences laboratory.

The IPO might also unleash a historic wave of philanthropy: all seven of Anthropic’s founders are likely to become billionaires and have pledged to donate 80% of their equity in the company to charity, including chief executive Dario Amodei. And on 18 October, the company announced that it had established the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, created to support initiatives that benefit society and stocked with an initial commitment of 5% of Anthropic’s shares.

But the firm has drawn criticism from researchers, who say its aims of curing diseases on short timescales are unrealistic and that its race towards developing ultra-powerful, ‘superintelligent’ AI models pose serious risks, including an existential threat to humanity. In its public prospectus, published ahead of the IPO, Anthropic outlines a new governance structure that it says is “consistent with our commitment to AI safety and responsibility”, and adds that safety research directly shapes the firm’s “model design, training, and deployment.”

Nature looks at four areas of science where Anthropic is making waves.

AI’s potential to turbocharge the discovery of new medicines has been a centerpiece of Anthropic’s pitch to investors. “If today we look at things like cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, mental illness — these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade,” Amodei said in a promotional video ahead of the IPO.

The company has been rapidly expanding its biomedical ambitions. This year, Anthropic opened its first ‘wet’ laboratory for life sciences research, announced partnerships with several pharmaceutical companies, and said it was pursuing drug leads of its own. “We plan to scale this work up substantially from here,” the company said on 27 October.

Anthropic bought a one-person, AI-powered biotech: is this drug discovery’s future?

Anthropic bought a one-person, AI-powered biotech: is this drug discovery’s future?

But Amodei’s habit of promising swift, AI-fueled cures for complex diseases has rankled many researchers and entrepreneurs in the field who feel the timeline is unrealistic.

Over the last year, Anthropic has made a major push in the life sciences. In June, the company hired John Jumper, who shared the 2024 Chemistry Nobel Prize for his work on AlphaFold2 while at Google DeepMind in London.

Some of the company’s early biological research received a mixed reception from biologists. After Anthropic reported using a swarm of AI agents to find signs of a new CRISPR-like system in viral sequence data, some researchers questioned the novelty of the finding and noted that the company had not carried out the experimental work needed to determine the system’s function.

In protein design — a field that has boomed thanks to specialist AI tools including AlphaFold — Anthropic’s work has also failed to generate much excitement. In August, Anthropic used Claude Science — an agentic system that can access other biological tools and databases — to make novel ‘binders’ against 15 protein targets.

“Expectations are sky high,” says Anthony Gitter, a computational biologist at the Morgridge Institute for Research in Madison, Wisconsin. “I understand why some view their initial public results as underwhelming.”

But Gitter is enthusiastic about Anthropic’s protein design efforts, largely because the company was transparent about the work, from the prompts it used to the sequences that were generated. “I would strongly encourage Anthropic to continue that in their future life sciences research,” Gitter adds.

In recent months, Anthropic and other companies — notably Google DeepMind and OpenAI — have been working to establish their research credentials in large part by showing off the rapidly growing mathematical abilities of their flagship AI models.

On 7 September Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge and collaborator Tristan Buckmaster at New York University solved a special case of the Navier-Stokes equations, a long-standing problem in mathematical physics that describes the flow of fluids. Hours after Anthropic announced the result, OpenAI claimed a full solution of the problem, igniting a controversy.

In another collaboration, Alpöge and mathematical physicist Ethan Sussman at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois, have been working towards establishing the mathematical foundations of the standard model of particle physics. This too is a problem on which OpenAI has made similar claims.

Anthropic and its competitors see the ability to write a rigorous proof of a mathematical fact as a crucial testing ground for their reasoning models. That’s in large part because the correctness of a proof is an objective measure that can be used as a ‘reward’ to further train AI systems.

#869. Mardle: The Worlds is now the 'incentive' for Littler

Sky Sports Darts' Wayne Mardle believes Luke Littler has to use winning the World Darts Championship as his motivation following his Grand Slam of Darts loss; you can watch the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports until November 22

Darts Expert & Columnist @Wayne501Mardle

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Luke Littler suffered a shock 10-8 defeat to Jermaine Wattimena at the last 16 stage of the Grand Slam of Darts and Sky Sports Darts' Wayne Mardle believes the world No 1 now has to throw all his energy into being ready for the World Darts Championship.

Littler was attempting to become the third player ever to win the Wolverhampton event three times in a row alongside Phil Taylor and Michael van Gerwen.

However, he came up against an incredible performance from Wattimena, in which he was hitting T20s for fun and averaged over 101.

With Littler also missing the Players Championship, which is the last major before Alexandra Palace in December, the next time we will see Littler on the TV stage is when he plays his opening Worlds match on Friday December 11 as the reigning champion, live on Sky Sports.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Littler went into 2026 targeting a clean sweep of majors and while he won the Premier League, Masters, UK Open, and World Matchplay, his loss in the second round at the World Series Finals to Dirk van Duijvenbode has started a run without a major win.

He has since not defended his World Grand Prix title, Grand Slam title, or clinched the European Championship, which has eluded him.

For Mardle, Littler has to put everything else to one side, use his time away to get fresh, practice, and win the major that just has something a bit different to the rest.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"There is no doubt that every player gets more motivated. The Worlds is different," Mardle said.

"The run-up is different and the build-up to it is gigantic.

"He went basically nine months into the year holding this belief and everyone else thinking he's going to do the clean sweep.

"So it was nine months of all this and then it ends, but the Worlds is out on its own. The incentive is that it is the Worlds. That is all the incentive you need. It is the biggest and it is the best event.

"If he loses in that then he will have gone four months without a major.

"The Worlds is the one, and Michael van Gerwen said this for years: what is the point in winning anything else? You only need to win this one.

"I think that is just the same with Luke's mentality."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

The talk has already turned to whether Littler's time away from the TV spotlight will be a positive or a negative as he attempts to become the second player ever, alongside Taylor, to have won the World Darts Championship three or more times in a row.

Mardle insists that, while it would be better for Littler to be heading into the Worlds as a potential Players Championship winner after his loss at the Grand Slam, if he brings his A-game, it is his to lose.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I don't know how he really feels about losing here at the Grand Slam but what I do think going forward, because he's not playing in the Players Championship, so his next outing will be at the Worlds.

"This is the way that I would frame it - would he be better not playing, or would he be better winning the Players Championship? You are better winning the Players Championship.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"But that is the kind of situation that you don't know. You don't know if he goes to the Players Championship, wins it or loses.

"If he loses, it is like maybe he shouldn't have gone to that, in hindsight and everything else.

"I really believe for Luke, if he can turn up fresh, if he can turn up ready, if he can turn up with anywhere near his A-game, he probably wins the Worlds again. That will be three times on the bounce by the age of 20, which is ridiculous."

Wattimena picked up the biggest win of his career against Littler at the Grand Slam but it is not the first time he has come out on top against 'The Nuke' as he beat him in August on the way to winning a Players Championship title.

Wattimena said that win gave him confidence and reinforced that Littler is "not a robot" and Mardle believes that win can be credited for the performance we saw from the Dutchman in the Grand Slam.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I know this is a thing. I was about when Phil Taylor was hardly ever beaten and until you actually beat him, you don't believe you can," he said.

"You see others beat him, there were loads throughout the years. There was Andy Callaby. Adrian Gray beat him. There were others that beat him that were not as good as me.

"I remember thinking why can't I ever beat Phil? It is not until you do that you know that someone's not a robot.

"So that win was massive for Jermaine and it was one of the reasons why he won yesterday.

"Now going forward after yesterday, he can beat anyone on that stage. Luke Humphries has to watch out if he plays Jermaine. Gerwyn Price, they should all watch out now.

"It is really important to have belief. Now he has got it and he has got the ability."

#867. FIA to introduce full-time F1 stewards

Formula 1's governing body, the FIA, has revealed full-time stewards will be used for the first time from next year; watch the Las Vegas GP weekend on Sky Sports F1, with Friday's practice sessions at 12.30am and 4pm

The FIA has announced it will introduce full-time Formula 1 stewards from 2027 with the aim of having "greater consistency in decision-making".

The use of full-time stewards has been a consistent talking point in F1 as different stewards, who adjudicate all racing and technical matters on a race weekend, are used at each event over the season.

There has been an argument that this can lead to inconsistencies in decision-making when it comes to imposing penalties, or the severity of a penalty.

But the FIA announced on Thursday, ahead of this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, they will begin to recruit full-time stewards with a phased introduction from next year with the aim of establishing 12-15 full-time stewards over the coming years.

Currently, there are four stewards drawn from a large FIA pool of officials and one of those is a former racing driver. The new structure will continue to use the knowledge of driver stewards at each event and the FIA say full-time stewards will "allow for deeper implementation of best practice and greater consistency in decision-making".

The news comes a month after the opening of the FIA Remote Operations Centre at Biggin Hill in the UK, following a reorganisation of Race Control in 2022 after the controversial 2021 season which saw Max Verstappen overtake Lewis Hamilton on the last lap of the season-ending Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.

"This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport," said FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.

"The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula One World Championship, it is also an investment in the future of our sport.

"Following the milestone opening of the new FIA Remote Operations Centre and strengthening of officiating development through initiatives such as the FIA High Performance Programme, this development will help to build greater expertise and continuity within our stewarding structure, strengthening our ability to review and improve regulations, support the development of future officials and ensure the highest standards of consistent officiating across all our championships."

#866. Overlap, underlap or sit back? How Premier League teams use their full-backs

The role of full-back has changed massively in recent years. We analyse how all 20 sides are approaching the position

Overlapping. Underlapping. Inverted. Traditional. The role of full-back has evolved dramatically. Once a defensive-first position that provided some auxiliary attacking support, the role has developed into something far more multifaceted.

Just ask right-back Ben White, who – with Riccardo Calafiori on the left – has been an important figure in Arsenal’s superb start to the campaign. Talking a few years ago, he said: “Playing full-back the way [Mikel Arteta] wants is completely different to any other manager. To play full-back for him, you’ve got to be a centre-midfielder, a centre-back, a winger and a No 10.”

Between them, White and Calafiori have contributed to six goals for Arsenal already in the Premier League this season (White: three assists; Calafiori: one goal, two assists). No other defender has registered more than three goal involvements so far. The Arsenal duo are a great illustration of the impact full-backs can have. But, with the position more demanding than ever before, how does each Premier League team deploy theirs?

The graphic below shows the average height and width of the touches of each Premier League team’s full-backs, sorted from highest average position to lowest. The most obvious takeaway is that Arsenal’s full-backs have the highest average touch location of any Premier League side this season, coming 58.2 metres from their own goal.

That is a reflection not only of Arsenal’s territorial dominance, but also the license White and Calafiori are given to push into the attacking line. White averages 3.4 touches in the opposition box per 90 minutes, the most of any full-back or wing-back in the division. Calafiori ranks third, with 2.9.

Arsenal’s full-backs also have the narrowest average touch locations of any team, emphasising how far they have moved away from the traditional full-back role of maintaining width. Instead, they are encouraged to drift inside and operate in central areas.

Tottenham also deploy their full-backs extremely high up the pitch. For most of the campaign, that has been Archie Gray at right-back and Andy Robertson on the left. Of course, analysing a player’s influence is not limited to what they do on the ball. Thanks to Opta Vision, we can also track what they do without it.

Gray is particularly noteworthy, given his exceptional work rate. He ranks first among Premier League full-backs for underlapping runs, both in total (23) and per 90 minutes (2.9), and also ranks fourth for overlapping runs per 90 (1.8). That shows the benefit of deploying an attack-minded player at full-back, with Gray showing energy and an ability to get beyond the ball and offer another option in the final third.

Robertson is no slouch on the opposite flank, either. The 32-year-old ranks seventh for underlapping runs per 90 minutes (1.4) and sits inside the top 20 for overlapping runs per 90 (1.1). He has also received more passes ending in the final third (159) than any other full-back.

It might be more of a surprise to see Coventry’s full-backs play so high, given they have not dominated the ball at all (39.1% possession, second-lowest) and they start their attacks from deep (40.2m away from goal, sixth-lowest). It is, however, something they did to good effect in the Championship last season (average height of 56.8m, sixth-highest).

Frank Lampard has also used a back five at times, which means his wing-backs naturally play higher up, but he has been brave with pushing his defensive line up in general. Coventry have provoked the second-most offsides of any team so far (30).

That has allowed Milan van Ewijk and Jay Dasilva to push forward on the flanks. The pair have each created eight chances, with only Jack Rudoni (12) creating more for the Sky Blues.

Dasilva is a particularly important outlet down the left. He takes his touches higher up the pitch than any other full-back in the division, and Coventry have created 42.2% of their open-play chances down his side, the highest proportion of any Premier League team.

It makes sense that Nottingham Forest and Leeds also see their full-backs touch the ball high up the pitch, given they are two of the biggest users of wing-backs. That pair are two of just four teams that predominantly play with wing-backs, with the back three/five becoming a rare breed in the modern Premier League.

For Leeds, Jayden Bogle has been particularly influential going forwards. He has made more runs ending in the opposition box than any other full-back this season. They’ve come at an average of 3.9 per 90 minutes, the second-highest rate in the division, behind only Nico O’Reilly, who has played just 54.3% of his minutes at full-back.

Crystal Palace, meanwhile, are feeling the effects of losing the influential Daniel Muñoz. Despite playing solely with wing-backs, they have gone from having the highest average full-back positioning in the Premier League in 2025-26 to sitting below the league average this season. Muñoz was relentless in his work up and down the right flank last term, and his absence has clearly affected the extent to which Palace are able to push their right-sided wing-back up in those wide areas.

The Colombian is now at Nottingham Forest with his former manager Oliver Glasner. They have gone from having the fifth-lowest average touch location for their full-backs to the fourth-highest. That is not only down to Muñoz, but having someone who is able to put in consistent lung-busting runs – he is behind only Ipswich Town’s Leif Davis for the average length of his off-ball runs – helps a lot.

We can’t talk about the league’s most energetic full-backs without mentioning Adrien Truffert, who has continued where he left off last season. The Frenchman is the overlapping king, making more of those runs than any other full-back in the division (23). That comes after he made almost twice as many overlapping runs as any other player across the entire league last season. His manager, Andoni Iraola, may be gone, but he’s clearly got the same license to bomb on from Bournemouth’s new head coach, Marco Rose.

Iraola is now at Liverpool, and his full-backs are one of the most asymmetric duos in the league. Milos Kerkez – just as he did at Bournemouth under Iraola – has freedom to push forward and is one of the biggest overlappers in the league, completing 15 such runs thus far. On the other side, Ronald Araújo – who is more of a converted centre-back – plays a far more reserved role.

Manchester City are a curious case. Despite averaging the most possession in the division (65.4%), completing the most passes per game (566) and recording the highest territorial dominance, as measured by field tilt, Enzo Maresca’s team do not use their full-backs in advanced areas to exert that dominance.

Their average full-back touch location is 53.1 metres from goal, making them the fourth-deepest team in the division. That is a huge contrast from Pep Guardiola’s last season, when City ranked third-highest for average full-back positioning. There are plenty of ways to play full-back in the Premier League, but the growing importance of the position is the same for every team.

#865. Nacua handed three-match suspension by NFL for policy violation

Puka Nacua won't miss any games that he wouldn't already miss because of injury; Nacua is eligible to return both from IR and his suspension when the Rams (6-4) host the Dallas Cowboys on December 20; watch the NFL throughout the season live on Sky Sports

Los Angeles Rams receiver Puka Nacua has been suspended for three games for violating the NFL's personal conduct policy.

The suspension begins immediately and Nacua will be eligible for reinstatement on December 14, following the Rams' Week 14 game against the San Francisco 49ers.

The All-Pro receiver won't be paid during his suspension but, thanks to the timing of his suspension, won't miss any games because he is currently out due to knee and toe injuries.

Nacua went on injured reserve last week and he is eligible to return from both IR and his suspension when the Rams (6-4) host the Dallas Cowboys on December 20.

The Rams and Nacua have been awaiting his probable suspension for nearly a year. The suspension of Nacua stems from an incident on New Year's Eve in 2025, where he allegedly made an antisemitic remark and bit a woman.

The accuser filed a civil lawsuit on March 25 against Nacua for assault and battery, while Nacua's attorney denied his client made any such statements and described the biting as "horseplay."

Nacua entered a holistic care facility earlier that month, before he was sued, the concluded his time in the rehab facility in time to be part of Los Angeles' off-season program in mid-April.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

He has appeared in seven games this season, despite battling multiple injuries. He has totalled 70 receptions for 715 yards this season, with four touchdowns.

Nacua also missed two games with a core muscle injury in September before hurting his knee on the final offensive play of the Rams' win at Washington on November 8.

#864. Former Spain midfielder Mata retires aged 38

Mata celebrates winning Euro 2012 with Spain

Former Spain midfielder Juan Mata has announced his retirement from playing at the age of 38.

Mata, who made 41 international appearances, was part of the Spain squad that won the 2010 World Cup, and he helped his country win the European Championship two years later when he scored in the 4-0 final victory against Italy.

A former Real Madrid youth player, he joined Valencia in 2007 before a move to Chelsea in August 2011 where he won the Champions League, Europa League and FA Cup.

Mata moved to Manchester United in January 2014 and helped them claim the Europa League, FA Cup and League Cup prior to his departure in 2022.

He went on to have spells at Turkish side Galatasaray and Vissel Kobe in Japan before he played for Australian sides Western Sydney Wanderers and Melbourne Victory.

"Football will never leave my life," said Mata. "There are so many ways to continue loving the game, so many ways to keep using it as a vehicle for development.

"I may stop playing professionally, but I will never stop being a footballer."

Mata was Chelsea's player of the year in both full seasons he was at Stamford Bridge. He made 82 league appearances for the club, scoring 18 goals.

"What a player," Chelsea posted on social media.

At Manchester United, he scored 51 goals in 285 outings before leaving after his contract expired.

"Congratulations on a fantastic career, Juan! Everyone at United wishes you all the best in your next steps," said United statement., external

#863. Manchester United’s infamous 1974 relegation is a warning from history

It may have been a different era, but the 1970s contain salutary lessons for a club in serious decline once again

In many ways, there are striking parallels between the Manchester United relegated in 1974 and the Manchester United sitting in the relegation zone at this stage of the season for the first time in 40 years. A legendary manager leaves, his shadow remains; with boardroom dithering and uncertainty, his replacements churn and burn as the club slide over several years.

Sir Matt Busby stepped aside as manager of the 1968 European Cup-winning side, but stayed on as a director, just as Sir Alex Ferguson did, watching from the Old Trafford directors’ box as successors tried and failed.

In the six years after being crowned kings of Europe, United turned to Wilf McGuinness, Busby stepped in temporarily to keep them up, then Frank O’Farrell was appointed before they landed on Tommy Docherty, who experienced the ignominy of taking them down.

In the past eight years, United have sacked José Mourinho, Ole Gunnar Solskjær, Erik ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and now Michael Carrick.

How did the United of 1974 go down? Most outsiders believed they were too big to fail. Inside the club, though, they sensed the direction of travel. After a heavy defeat at Crystal Palace in December 1972, Busby offered Docherty the job in the Selhurst Park boardroom. “There’s a lot of trouble in the camp,” Busby said. Docherty was doing well as Scotland manager and took a few days to mull it over, but decided he couldn’t turn down the opportunity.

When Busby called him on the Sunday evening, he accepted. “You know it won’t be easy?” Busby said. “It’ll be like turning an oil tanker round, only bigger.” He added: “You might find yourself having to take a step back in order to take a leap forward.” Docherty wrote in his autobiography, The Doc, that at the time he never believed Busby was alluding to relegation.

Docherty was given free rein for a rebuild. The day after his appointment, he signed George Graham from Arsenal for £120,000, a sizeable fee at the time. Alex Forsyth followed from Partick for £100,000 and Docherty pulled off a coup when he persuaded Lou Macari to join bottom-of-the-table United instead of Liverpool for £200,000.

The giants of the previous era were moved on. In February, Bobby Charlton told him that, at 37, it would be his last season. Other big names wanted to stay, but Docherty felt a reset was needed. “The Manchester United team that had won the European Cup in 1968 was without a doubt a great team, but many members of that side had been allowed to grow old together,” he wrote.

“I knew what I had decided would prove very unpopular with many people but it had to be done. I set out my stall to end the United careers of among others Denis Law, Tony Dunne, Pat Crerand and David Sadler.”

George Best, who had retired once but returned under Docherty, played his last game on New Year’s Day 1974 after repeatedly turning up late. The most controversial departure was Law, who was allowed to join Manchester City.

Having taken over with United bottom, Docherty kept them up in his first season and was emboldened to continue his clearout. Thirteen players were released that summer. But halfway through the following season they were facing relegation again and a lack of goals cost them. At one stage, the joint-top scorer was Alex Stepney, with two penalties. He was the goalkeeper.

Relegation was confirmed on the penultimate day as they lost to City, a defeat made all the more painful by Law back-heeling the late winner. Docherty was interviewed on the Old Trafford pitch and asked, in a scene replayed in TNT Sports’ Too Good To Go Down, whether the club would drift into obscurity. “No, there’s no danger,” he said. “We could wash the jerseys here and hang them out to dry and you’d get 15,000 people standing watching them do so.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Despite the bravado, Docherty was expecting the sack when he met Busby a few days later. Instead, Busby handed him a case of champagne, reminded him of the oil tanker and told him to set to work getting them back up.

Docherty’s prediction proved right: the brand was far bigger than the division they played in. In the Second Division, Old Trafford averaged crowds of more than 47,000 – the biggest in the country – and their away support descended on towns and cities and routinely outnumbered the home contingent.

Docherty bought young and hungry, targeting players with a point to prove, including Steve Coppell from Tranmere, Stuart Pearson from Hull and Jim Holton from Shrewsbury. The direct, attacking football synonymous with United returned and the Scot shaped a fearless 4-2-4 formation.

Crowds grew after they came straight back up and for a while United were on course to become the fifth side to win the First Division after promotion, but finished third and also reached the FA Cup final, losing 1-0 to Southampton. That shows the stark differences between then and now.

The gap between the first and second tiers was narrower. United did not lose a gargantuan broadcast deal when they went down. They were not saddled with debt by their owners. Their wage bill was not tied to Champions League qualification. Players were not on long contracts and were easier to buy and sell. There were no disruptive agents. Fans were more patient.

If lessons of the 1970s are not heeded soon, the fallout could be infinitely more painful.
