#862. Inside women’s football’s difficult rise in Syria: ‘A joy that everyone in the country needed’

A 14-year civil war ravaged the country and ground women’s football to a halt. Today, the first glimmers of hope are beginning to emerge amid difficulty

In December 2024, Syria’s under-18 women’s football team boarded a last-minute bus at midnight from Aqaba, bound for Damascus. The players had been in Jordan preparing for their final match of the WAFF women’s championship, where a win against Saudi Arabia would have kept their hopes of winning the title alive. Syria pulled out amid fears that the border would close.

Back home, a war that had been largely frozen for four years was suddenly moving at pace. Rebel forces had swept out of the northwest, taking Aleppo and were pushing south towards the capital, 350km away, threatening to topple the now-former president, Bashar al-Assad. Players from the provinces around Damascus made their way home. But those from Hasakah, in the country’s far north-east, spent the next three days stranded at Damascus airport, as airline staff fled and planes sat idle on the tarmac, until a bus was finally able to take them home.

Scared, exhausted and running on adrenaline, the team had lived through another episode of disruption; but in truth they had rarely known stability. For Syrian women’s footballers, navigating uncertainty had been part of the game long before the country’s political upheaval reached its latest turning point. “My generation was burned away and completely lost,” said Noor Jumaa, a former national team goalkeeper. “It was like everything that was being built just disappeared.”

After 14 years of war, Syria has much to rebuild. Women’s football is among the institutions trying to recover from a conflict that erased an entire generation of players, interrupted the development of the game itself and left its infrastructure struggling. Yet, in recent years, Syria’s youth teams have emerged as one of the country’s more unexpected sporting success stories, winning regional titles and producing players who are beginning to make their mark abroad.

Syria’s women’s national team played their first international match in 2005. By 2011, plans were under way for an 11-a-side women’s league. Then the uprising began, and all plans were abandoned. For the next six years, women’s football in Syria effectively stopped. There were no international fixtures at any level, only occasional futsal tournaments. More than six million people eventually fled Syria, including hundreds involved in the sport, leaving an already small pool of players scattered across the world.

Men’s football, by contrast, continued. The national team played matches abroad after Syria was barred from hosting fixtures in 2011 on security grounds. The Assad regime used its successes to project an image of normality, even welcoming the squad to his palace after their 2012 WAFF Championship victory. Fifa, despite its rules against political interference, stayed silent.

Girls growing up in those years had no women’s team to watch. “I was watching a match of Syria’s men’s national team, and I was really upset. I would say, ‘God, if only they’d make a national team for girls,’” recalled Raneem Abo Lateef, a 21-year-old goalkeeper for Syria. The opportunity came unexpectedly after her family moved houses, and a girl next door told Abo Lateef that a relative was starting a girls’ club. “Girls’ football? Wow,” she said. “It was like dreams coming true.”

Similarly, international teammate Julnar Mustafa spent hours playing with boys in her neighbourhood in Hasakah. Born in 2008, so too young to remember the beginning of the uprising, she filmed herself dribbling and performing tricks on her phone, uploading the videos to Facebook. A regional coach came across them and invited Mustafa to join his team.

But finding an opportunity to play was only part of the challenge. “In our society, especially in the north, in Hasakah, sport is completely off-limits for girls,” Mustafa told the Guardian. “Not football, not anything”.

While a new generation of girls were finding their way into football, the national team was attempting to return to international competition. In April 2017, Syria entered the Asian Cup qualifiers in Vietnam, assembling a squad after six years without any activity. The federation announced tryouts on Facebook, and players were given about a month of preparation. Syria went on to lose every match, including a 14-0 defeat by Myanmar. “Honestly, it was one of the worst teams in Syria’s history,” said Jumaa, who was part of that squad. “We lost by terrifying scores.”

Maha Al-Katreb, also in the squad at the time, remembers the criticism that followed. Players were ridiculed despite having had little preparation. At the tournament, she saw opponents arrive with larger coaching staffs and younger players training alongside their senior teams. The gap between Syria and their regional competitors was difficult to ignore.

With injuries ending her career early, Al-Katreb fell into coaching by chance and turned towards building a programme that could develop the next generation. She later joined the Syrian Football Association (SFA), taking on administrative and coaching responsibilities.

A six-team women’s senior league was established in 2019, followed by the development of youth national teams. This year the country held an inaugural edition of its youth league. Al-Katreb developed Syria’s first women’s football strategy, submitted to Fifa, that set out a longer-term plan for expanding participation and creating a pathway into the national teams. “You have to start building from the bottom if you want to see results after these 10 years,” Al-Katreb said. “So that we don’t burn one generation after another.”

In 2022, women accounted for only 1,000 of Syria’s 25,000 registered footballers. The women’s football strategy, seen by the Guardian, aimed to increase female participation by 150% over four years, including through 33 school training centres across 11 provinces, with capacity for 1,650 girls by 2026.

The government has also outlined plans to rehabilitate the country’s sporting infrastructure. Rami Alsubea, an adviser at the Ministry of Sport and Youth, said in a statement that 48 sports facilities had been rehabilitated in 2025, with plans to rehabilitate about 150 more and build about 20 new ones by 2028. Restoring infrastructure is in part to meet hosting criteria set by Fifa and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC).

Al-Katreb left the federation more than a year ago. Jumaa is now part of a two-woman team leading its women’s football department, appointed after the arrival of the federation’s current president, Feras al-Teet. Several players have criticized the federation’s leadership and the pace of progress. The Guardian reached out to Al-Teet for comment. He declined.

Among the players who have been vocal about the shortcomings is 26-year-old Rona Aizouk, one of the most experienced members of the current generation. Named after Brazilian footballer Ronaldinho, she made history in 2023 when she became the first Syrian-born woman to sign a professional contract, joining Saudi side Najmat Jeddah. Her performances in Syria had attracted the club’s attention, but securing the move proved difficult. Visa refusals and paperwork complications delayed her arrival until two days before the season began. Her time in Saudi Arabia lasted only a few months, and she was unable to extend her stay.

“Honestly, I went there not wanting to come back,” said Aizouk. “There’s no comparison. Everything is better, the treatment, the training, the facilities. It’s just different.

“The most important thing is the players’ comfort. Here in Syria, we have to endure psychological pressure and torment. As a player, I have to fight the world just to achieve even a little bit of success.”

After returning to Damascus to complete her studies, Aizouk quickly received interest from multiple clubs in Jordan, where she now plays. For her, being in situ abroad is about more than personal progression. “I want to be a message that I, who came out of hard circumstances and out of a war, still managed to succeed.”

Aizouk’s exposure to regional excellence has shown her that Syria is still many years behind. At the forefront is financial restriction that has left the sport bare-boned. International sanctions and banking restrictions imposed on Syria left millions of dollars in development funding from Fifa inaccessible to the SFA, preventing it from fully benefiting from programmes such as Fifa Forward.

Although broad economic sanctions have since been lifted, an estimated $11.5m in funds remains inaccessible to the federation. Both the SFA and Fifa insist they are working to establish a mechanism through which the money can be transferred. For now, the support has been seen in training equipment.

The financial strain is felt directly by players as both the national team and regional league are operated by the SFA. Clubs frequently go months without paying wages, and when payments do arrive, players say they can fall short of the amounts agreed. International call-ups offer little relief: during national team duty, including training camps, players receive a daily allowance of $20, capped at $200 for the length of their stay, regardless of how long it is. Some say the costs of travelling and playing can exceed what they receive.

Several clubs have folded since the domestic league’s launch in 2019, citing financial difficulties and the continued disruption caused by the war and ongoing conflicts. Those that remain often struggle to provide even basic resources.

Al-Hilal, now renamed Qamishlo Sport, have become one of the country’s most successful women’s sides, currently reigning as senior and youth league champions. But their achievements have not translated into financial security, according to head coach, Daleel Khalid. “There’s an absence of adequate support from all sides and the parties responsible for Syrian women’s sports, whether in terms of training camps and preparation, or the capabilities and infrastructure needed to develop the game,” he said.

The club’s campaign at the 2026 WAFF Women’s Clubs Championship was a big test. The tournament brought together league champions from six regional competitions. Despite having only a short training camp at home, Al-Hilal reached the final against Saudi champions Al-Nassr. Abo Lateef and Mustafa were among those who represented them, and their performances offered a reminder that Syrian teams can compete with the region’s best, even when their opponents have considerably greater resources.

There was also individual recognition. Al-Hilal’s Mai Al-Jani was named the tournament’s best player after a series of standout performances, an achievement she was quick to share with those around her. “The award I won is a source of pride for me, for the club and for the players. I see it as a team award,” she said. “It belongs to the staff, the players, and every Syrian girl living through these difficult circumstances.”

Born in 2006 in a small village in Homs province, Al-Jani has emerged as one of Syria’s promising attacking talents. She won the league’s Golden Boot in the 2024-25 season and has continued to impress for both club and country. She was also named the best player at the 2023 WAFF under-17 championship, when Syria won their first international title in women’s football. Al-Katreb, who was an assistant coach, saw the victory as evidence of what the country could build with the right support.

The WAFF under-17 triumph was repeated at the 2026 edition with a completely different squad. “It was joy that everyone in the country needed,” said Jumaa. “We were completely outnumbered in technical and admin staff, with only nine of us managing everything. Other teams had double the number of staff, with gameplay technology we can’t get our hands on.”

For Abo Lateef, the greatest risk is allowing another generation of players to lose the chance to compete. The senior women’s national team, for instance, has not played in over two years, with no reason given to players. “We need competition, regardless of the level,” said Abo Lateef. “I’m afraid a day will come when I’m made to sit at home, as was the case with the ones before us. A friendly fixture is a good start. Anything.”

Aizouk’s message to those responsible for the future of the women’s game was more direct. “Save Syrian football,” she said. “Save the generations. Save us.”

#861. Drone footage of Pochettino's first Man Utd training session leaked online

A 12-minute video of Mauricio Pochettino's first training session as Manchester United boss has been leaked online, showing the new head coach doing training drills ahead of Sunday's match against Liverpool at Anfield, which is live on Sky

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Mauricio Pochettino’s first Manchester United training session today has been leaked online in a major security breach.

The 12-minute drone footage over their Carrington training ground was uploaded onto YouTube.

It shows Pochettino doing various tactical drills with his new team as they prepare for their clash with Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday.

United have signs around the Carrington area warning that use of drones are "strictly prohibited" and anyone caught "will be reported for prosecution and subject to civil action".

The uploaders of the drone footage, CC Overview, claimed to have not breached any laws.

On the video they posted: "For the people asking about legality. It is unrestricted airspace, meaning anyone can fly over it, the drone remained in line of sight at all times, it didn't fly over anyone or even near anyone so was a perfectly legal flight going by the CAA rules that regulates drone usage.

"The drone is correctly labelled and I hold all the relevant licences, public liability and insurance required.

"As for leaking team news/ tactics, it was half an hour into the manager's first training session, there are many media there so certainly won't be the only footage of training released."

The training today was a closed session and not open to the media.

Manchester United declined to comment when contacted by Sky Sports News.

"This 12-minute video starts off innocuously. We see large numbers of Man Utd players on a separate pitch doing what is known as rondos, those small groups of six or seven players with one or two in the middle trying to intercept the ball. It's the classic pre-training warm-up. That's pretty innocuous. That won't give Liverpool or anyone else much of an insight into what Pochettino's tactical thinking might be for his first game in charge.

"But then on the next pitch, as the drone moves across, it zooms in, and the zoom is quite incredible. You can make out faces and we see Pochettino hands-on, walking them through certain match scenarios. At one stage Pochettino calls all those players in for a huddle and a briefing.

"I'm not going to give you any information about who those players are. But these 11 players Pochettino calls in - 10 outfield players and one goalkeeper. We shouldn't assume this is his starting XI, necessarily.

"Saturday would be the day we'd expect United to do their specific tactics and shape to prepare for the game at Anfield the next day. If this was drone footage of that session it would be even more damaging, even more explosive.

"But the fact it's 11 players separated from the group... it's a very difficult situation for Pochettino and Manchester United.

"I don't think [Pochettino and the players] were aware of it at the time.

"It's questionable whether the person handling the drone has done anything illegal. All around Carrington training ground, they have a large numbers of signs up saying drones are prohibited. But it's clear from these images the drone was not flying directly above United's property. It was to the side of United's property and zoomed in.

"There's absolutely no suggestion Liverpool are involved in this, they are clearly not. But you have to say, it could be advantageous to Liverpool and Andoni Iraola if he's planning his tactics for Sunday's game to look at this and get an idea of how Manchester United might be lining up and what Pochettino might be thinking.

"While it seems as though there are probably no laws that have been broken here, nevertheless it's an awful lot of very specific footage which Manchester United and Pochettino would not want out in the public.

"If you look at the impact of what we're talking about, Man Utd earlier today released some images of the training session and it showed Harry Maguire and Patrick Dorgu among the main training group. Both of those have had injury concerns of late. So those official images told me, Man Utd supporters and Liverpool's tactical preparation experts that Maguire and Dorgu may be in line for possible selection.

"It's gone a stage further now with this leaked drone footage because that has shed even more light on that. It gives a pretty clear picture of who's fit, who's out on the training field, who's involved and who isn't.

"That has to be a significant tactical advantage to Andoni Iraola and Liverpool as they go into this huge game on Sunday."

#860. Maine Road offer non-league haven to fans of scandal-hit Manchester City

Tenth-tier club aim to become a new home for disillusioned supporters and those priced out of the Premier League

It began with a timely message on social media. “We’ve seen the posts. We’ve read the comments. If all the recent conversation has made you curious about the other team in Manchester playing in sky blue, come and see us.”

It was a direct response to the news of a guilty verdict in the Premier League’s financial fair play case against Manchester City and it came from the 10th-tier (step six) club Maine Road, who carry City’s colours and a near-identical badge, as well as the name of City’s previous home.

Maine Road stadium was demolished in 2003-04 and replaced by houses but two miles away, in a corner of Chorlton-cum-Hardy, Maine Road FC are playing in front of about 100 people on a cool November Saturday. The high-stakes surroundings of the Premier League seem a fair distance away, but Maine Road – founded in 1955 in Rusholme as a Manchester City supporters’ club team – have never professed to be City.

“There is FC United and Manchester United, who are intrinsically linked in terms of why that club exists,” says Rob McKay, Maine Road women’s head coach, watching as a fan as the men’s side draw 0-0 with Halewood Apollo in the North West Counties League First Division North. “This is not a protest club. The links with City have ebbed and flowed over the years. It’s just that they were playing out of the Maine Road social club when it formed.”

The chair and director Alex Simmonds, who arrived in the summer, has big ambitions for Maine Road. He believes the fallout from City’s legal battle with the Premier League could help attract a new audience.

“It was a bit of a statement,” Simmonds says of that social media post. “We came across a lot of comments when the news came out and a lot were saying: ‘Well, we’ll stop watching City if they get relegated or if anything happens, and we’ll just go to Maine Road.’ That came up in quite a few conversations online.”

Simmonds admits there has not yet been a huge rise in crowd numbers, with City fans, perhaps understandably, staying defiantly loyal to their club, who have appealed against the independent commission’s verdict. His priority is to regenerate Maine Road. “For me coming into the club, it was about trying to get people to see that we are here,” he says. “To get in touch with the community and to get fans down here, so no matter who you support in the Premier League or Championship or whatever, we are here.”

Maine Road offer free entry to anyone with a season ticket for a Premier League or EFL club, hoping to boost numbers during international breaks or when other Greater Manchester teams play away. Simmonds is helping to fund a multimillion-pound renovation of St Margaret’s Community Centre, which serves as Maine Road’s clubhouse. The club are also launching a new website and a scheme to hand out thousands of free tickets to local primary schools.

Will that, combined with potential disillusionment after any City punishment, bring fans flocking to Maine Road? “I think it will,” Simmonds says, “but only if people know that there’s a difference between a Premier League Man City and a Maine Road at step six. If they come with ideas that we are going to be a City or even one of the bigger semi-pro teams … we’re not quite there yet. But their support would help.”

Non-league football in Greater Manchester has enjoyed a significant surge in popularity since Covid, so Maine Road find themselves in a crowded marketplace. McKay says: “West Didsbury and Chorlton are down the road and they get 1,000. Droylsden get huge crowds, Ashton United get huge crowds, Curzon Ashton are getting reasonable crowds. There’s so much football.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Simmonds believes the connection with City, however loose, should help Maine Road gradually gain a foothold. City’s former training ground at Platt Lane is a stone’s throw from Brantingham Road, where Maine Road play. City’s academy teams have played at Maine Road’s ground, as well as at nearby St Bede’s College.

Another connection is the fact Maine Road are managed by a former City player in Leon Mike, who made his only City start at the old Maine Road in 2001 under Kevin Keegan.

“People make jokes about the Etihad not being full, but genuinely, a lot of times you speak to City fans, they’ll say it’s too expensive,” says Mike. “Premier League, FA Cup, League Cup, Champions League, that’s a lot of games to go to. Whereas on a Saturday here it will cost you £6 to attend and you can have a pint and some food.”

There is optimism among those most closely connected with Maine Road that the club will soon experience growth. “We gained 9,000 followers across the platforms just on the back of that one social media post,” Simmonds says. “It was surprising – I didn’t think it would do that – but social media is really powerful. We’re definitely going to try and stay in that conversation and get people coming through.”

#858. Arsenal outclassed in defeat to dominant Lyon

Arsenal Women vs Olympiques Lyon Women. Women's Champions League.

Arsenal register a single shot on target, which came in stoppage-time, as they were outclassed by Lyon at Meadow Park; Jule Brand and Melchie Dumornay scored in each half but the French side could easily have finished with more goals in what was a dominant performance

Arsenal’s hopes of automatic qualification to the Women’s Champions League quarter-finals are hanging by a thread after they were beaten 2-0 at home by a dominant Lyon in foggy conditions.

The French side, who beat Arsenal in the semi-finals last season, got the better of the Gunners again at Meadow Park on Thursday night with goals from Jule Brand and Melchie Dumornay in each half sealing the victory.

Arsenal barely laid a glove on Lyon - who are yet to concede a goal in this season's Champions League - and now sit eighth in the standings, three points adrift of fourth-placed Chelsea, after their first loss in five league phase matches.

Emily Fox registered Arsenal's only shot on target of the game deep in stoppage-time and the home side could easily have conceded a few more had Marie-Antoinette Katoto not spurned two big opportunities.

Arsenal were also indebted to their goalkeeper, Misa, who produced three big saves in the second half to keep out Tabitha Chawinga, Dumornay and Vicki Becho.

Renee Slegers' side, now without a win in three matches in all competitions, are relying on teams above them to drop points in the final round of matches to avoid having to face a play-off match to secure their passage to the quarter-finals.

Meanwhile, Lyon, who currently sit second in the table, have secured a top-four finish with a game to spare after picking up 13 points from five matches.

Arsenal Women boss Renee Slegers to ESPN:

"Tough battle. Congratulations to Lyon who were better than us today. They play good football, physically strong in the duels, fast with the ball and without the ball.

"We had a tough time dealing with it in the first half. Second half we controlled the game better without creating clear-cut chances.

"But then you see how clinical Lyon were from their moments."

On her half-time team talk: "It was 1-0, so we were in the game. Like they had, we need moments as well. We are going to get moments and then how we are going to create it."

Sky Sports News reporter Uma Gurav at Meadow Park:

"The bigger picture here is that Arsenal have played the best two teams in this competition in two consecutive weeks and they've got just one point out of the two games.

"You have to admit the draw was very tough on them to get both Barcelona and Lyon, but it's also a harsh reality check.

"This Arsenal team won the Champions League just 18 months ago. Now, they're not quite up there with the European elites. Can they get back there anytime soon?"

Ex-Arsenal striker Lianne Sanderson to ESPN:

"I like Renee but there has to come a time [when we question] why is it that all the players look out of form? Apart from Alessia Russo, how many of those players are actually performing?

"There has to come a point where you have to start questioning Renee. As much as I like Renee and everything she's done.

"Not to compare the two, but it feels like Michael Carrick at Man Utd where you feel like someone has taken the team so far but now what?

"We're all waiting for Arsenal to kick on. That tonight disappointed me because it looked flat."

#855. ‘An honour’: Pochettino up for challenge of leading Manchester United revival

New head coach faces tough opening match at Anfield

‘It’s a big challenge but at the same time it’s adrenaline’

Mauricio Pochettino said it was “an honour” and “a privilege” to be the new Manchester United head coach after arriving in England on Wednesday.

Pochettino flew from Cincinnati to Manchester overnight after overseeing the USA beating Haiti in his final game in charge. Members of Pochettino’s staff landed earlier in the week to begin work at Carrington, laying the foundations as United seek to turn their season around. His right-hand man, Jesús Pérez, the goalkeeping coach Toni Jiménez and the fitness coach Sebastiano Pochettino, who continues to work with his father, have already taken training with those not on international duty.

Those away with their national teams will return to the club on Thursday, when they are expected to meet Pochettino for the first time and hold meetings. Conversations have also been held with various departments within the club, as Pochettino sought to learn about the squad’s health as he seeks areas of improvement.

Pochettino’s first challenge will be at Anfield on Sunday, when 18th-placed United take on Liverpool. The 54-year-old has his eyes set on rattling Manchester City after being told on TNT Sports that “Manchester’s blue and always will be blue” by DaMarcus Beasley, who once had a loan spell with City. Pochettino responded: “No way. You will see. Give me time … give me time and that is going to start to change.”

Speaking about joining United, Pochettino said: “It’s a big challenge but at the same time, it’s adrenaline that you want to feel because I think we are going to have a different job. But I think one of the things that is important is that we have the experience to deal with that, and I think we need to add our common sense and the way we are going to approach all the things.

“We know that the situation is not a situation that a club like Manchester United deserves,” Pochettino added. “The fanbase is amazing and after we signed here in America, of every 10 people I crossed in the street, nine are Manchester United fans. It’s amazing.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Pochettino is also reunited with the strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya, the analyst Alec Scott and his long-term assistant, Miki D’Agostino, at Old Trafford.

#850. Emma Hayes to assist in US Soccer hiring process for next USMNT coach

US women’s head coach won Olympics in 2024

Hayes enjoyed trophy-laden tenure at Chelsea

The US women’s national team head coach, Emma Hayes, said she was “confident in the group that is being put together” to select her next counterpart for the men’s team – a group that includes her.

Speaking after announcing her team’s squad for the ­Concacaf championship and World Cup qualifier, Hayes shed light for the first time on her role in searching for Mauricio Pochettino’s replacement after the Argentinian decamped to Manchester United. US Soccer had previously said Hayes – alongside the federation CEO, JT Batson, the chief operating officer, Dan Helfrich, and Oguchi Onyewu, the vice-president of sporting – would assist with the search.

“Listen, I’m very embedded into the federation, and I work really closely with JT, in particular, and even more so with Dan as we’re growing to develop the American soccer movement,” Hayes said. “And you know, JT asked if I would be involved as a technical voice to be involved with the process. And I feel confident in the group of people that have been put together to create a thorough process to select the next men’s national team coach – my role is merely to support that through a technical lens, knowing I do this job … albeit with the women’s team, and that I’ve coached for a number of years, and can offer some of that insight into the application of what to look for and why.”

Hayes résumé spans 25 years and is distinguished, having coached at the very highest level for club and country alike. The Englishwoman, who took over the US team in 2024, moved from being the assistant coach at Arsenal to taking charge of the Chicago Red Stars in Women’s Professional Soccer in 2008, and later moved to Chelsea, winning the Women’s Super League seven times. Since accepting the US job, she has guided the women to an Olympic gold medal and taken on an expansive role at the federation as it looks to overhaul and grow the women’s game.

“I think it will be a very thorough process,” Hayes said. “I think that’s the most important part of it. I feel very embedded in what we’re doing with the federation, so it doesn’t feel unusual to me [to help with the search]. So, like I’ve said many times, let’s build off the good work that Mauricio has done. I think that’s the important part, and let’s get it right.”

Hayes offered a heartfelt goodbye to Pochettino on the TNT broadcast of the his final match with the USMNT on Tuesday night, a 2-0 victory over Haiti in their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final. “I just want to say thank you on behalf of all of us at US Soccer, it’s been a privilege to work with you here, see the amazing work you’ve done with the team,” she said. “I think you’ve left an amazing foundation for someone to come in and build on that great work and the good feeling and certainly the good habits you’ve left with the team. You’ve left a lasting impression on the American people.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Pochettino replied on the broadcast, saying: “I admire a lot Emma. She is a wonderful coach, and a wonderful person. It was an honor to share [this experience] with her.”

#849. Russell fastest as rain limits running in Las Vegas GP practice

George Russell topped second practice from Pierre Gasly after there was very little running in first practice on a wet first day on track action; watch the Las Vegas GP on Sky Sports F1, with qualifying at 4am on Saturday and the race at 4am on Sunday

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Mercedes' George Russell topped Practice Two from Alpine's Pierre Gasly as rain limited running on the opening day of track action at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

After no timed laps were completed in first practice due to heavy rain falling throughout, the weather relented to allow plenty of running during the second session, albeit on a damp, slowly drying circuit that prevented the use of slick tyres.

The best lap times came at the end of the session, which took place on Thursday night in Las Vegas, when Russell pipped Gasly by 0.071s, with Ferrari's Charles Leclerc three tenths off the pace in third.

Leclerc and McLaren's Lando Norris, who won last time out in Brazil, had traded the fastest times for most of the session in the wetter conditions.

Norris ended up seventh, behind Red Bull's Isack Hadjar, his McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, but the times are likely to matter very little given qualifying and the race are expected to take place in dry conditions.

The schedule in Las Vegas runs a day earlier than a traditional F1 weekend, but the time difference means qualifying will take place at 4am on Saturday morning for UK viewers, with the race following at the same time on Sunday.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Remarkably, there were few incidents and the only red flag across the whole day was for a plastic bag blowing onto the circuit at the high-speed final corner in second practice.

New F1 world champion Kimi Antonelli was eighth fastest but will serve a five-place grid penalty after exceeding his internal combustion engine allocation for a second time this season.

Piastri, Williams' Carlos Sainz and Aston Martin's Lance Stroll have 10-place grid penalties for going over various power unit elements, while Haas' Oliver Bearman will start at the back.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Max Verstappen spent most of the day in the garage and completed only 10 laps in total as he finished second practice in 13th.

Verstappen, who is on a run of eight consecutive podiums, felt he had "no power" from the engine on the laps he completed and insisted "it was not normal" despite his engineer suggesting the issue was related to the power unit needing to warm up in the cold condtions.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

McLaren and Mercedes have brought upgrades this weekend but the rain on Thursday meant it was virtually impossible to tell whether they made any impact.

Final practice, which gets under way at 12.30am on Saturday for UK viewers, is set to be very busy as the drivers will attempt to get plenty of dry laps in before qualifying.

#848. Leicester part ways with BC Game after sponsor’s partnership with porn actor

Cryptocurrency casino made Eva Elfie a brand ambassador

Club end deal early citing ‘differing commercial priorities’

Leicester City have ditched their front-of-shirt sponsor, BC Game, after the cryptocurrency casino’s partnership with a porn actor sparked a fan backlash. BC Game, an offshore company registered in Belize that is unlicensed to operate in the UK, had been Leicester’s main sponsor since 2024.

This month BC Game named Eva Elfie a brand ambassador, leading the Foxes Trust, Leicester’s supporters’ trust, to highlight the “devastating impacts” caused by gambling and pornography. On Wednesday the club said they prematurely ended their agreement with the online betting firm after they “recognised our differing commercial priorities”.

It is understood Leicester directly raised concerns with BC Game about the implications of their deal with Elfie, a Russian porn actor who BC Game said had “an established presence in gaming communities”. Leicester’s deal with BC Game, which began in July 2024, was due to run until the end of the season.

The trust had previously outlined concerns about the club’s partnership with BC Game. In a statement responding to the partnership this month, they said: “From the moment the club decided to take sponsorship from a betting company we felt Leicester City were ditching its values.

“Now throw into the mix that BC Game have entered into a partnership with someone who continues to make their name via adult content. Partnerships like these bring these two worlds to a larger audience and, by association, link them to Leicester City. Is this who we are now?”

Leicester, who visit Huddersfield in League One on Saturday, said supporters who purchased a shirt featuring BC Game branding within the past 28 days are able to exchange the shirt or are eligible for a full refund. The club added they would pay for the postage of returns via standard delivery.

Leicester remain for sale, with the club’s Thai owners, King Power, also seeking to sell their stadium, training base and women’s team.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

In an unrelated development, the former Chelsea technical director Michael Emenalo is working as an adviser to the club, who are 11th in the third tier. Emenalo is among a team of Deloitte consultants Leicester say they have enlisted to “assess its current operations and inform its future strategic planning”.

#847. Taylor Swift CMA Awards Performance: Every Easter Egg

Taylor Swift made her return to the CMA Awards Nov. 18 after 10 years with a medley of “I Knew It, I Knew You” and “Our Song,” and her devoted fanbase has already found several Easter eggs.

It looks like Taylor Swift still has plenty of tricks up her sleeve—or rather snakes in her boot?

As the “I Knew It, I Knew You” singer took the stage at the CMA Awards Nov. 18 to perform a medley of her newest country hit as well as one of her first, “Our Song,” many fans noticed there may be several Easter eggs hinting at the re-release of her debut album.

The first clue fans noticed was dropped before Swift even started singing, as she began her performance in a backstage dressing room that was decorated with several familiar pieces of clothing, namely dresses she wore during her first rodeo.

For one, there was the butter yellow ballgown she wore to the CMA Awards in 2007—the year she scored her very first win—that was strewn across the couch behind Swift. Then, hanging on a clothing rack to her right, was a floral print halter dress that Swift wore to the Academy of Country Music Awards in 2006, which was one of the very first major red carpet walks of her career.

Even more noteworthy were the final two dresses fans noticed. One purple-looking dress that was directly behind Swift on a couch, mostly obscured from sight, appeared to be the fluffy strapless number she wore for a portion of the music video “Our Song.”

Meanwhile, the final dress was most obvious: the teal ballgown Swift wore not only in the “Teardrops on my Guitar” music video, but also to the Country Music Television Awards in 2007, when she won for Breakthrough Music Video of the Year Award for “Tim McGraw.”

But Swift’s old wardrobe weren’t the only Easter eggs Swifties spotted. Swift’s choreography appeared to walk her through the many eras of her career, including a red cowboy hat to denote her fourth studio album, as well as a pair of sunglasses briefly worn as a callback to the opening performance of her 1989 World Tour.

And the inclusion of several country music stars including Brad Paisley, Little Big Town, Sugarland, Brooks & Dunn, Eric Church, Lainey Wilson and Keith Urban led many fans to believe that the singers might be featured on vault tracks of the upcoming debut rerelease. (FWIW, however, Swift also has deep ties to many of these country stars, having covered or penned songs with or for several of them.)

Of course, Swift also included plenty of nods to Toy Story 5, the film for which she and Jack Antonoff wrote “I Knew It, I Knew You” for. In the dressing room at the beginning of the performance, a Jessie doll can be seen propped on one of the couches. And once Swift makes it to the stage, her blue guitar was adorned with Toy Story’s signature white clouding, while a tree with a tire swing engraved with the words “Jessie was here” was placed behind her.

Although Swifties have called Easter egg many times before, Swift has been teasing the release of her debut album since she confirmed she had purchased her master recordings back in May 2025. While the purchase signified the end of her Taylor’s Version era, she did admit that her first album was not only done, but would have its moment to “re-emerge when the time is right, if that would be something you guys would be excited about.”

Naturally, Swift doesn’t need question her fans’ enthusiasm toward that idea. Keep reading for more stars who stepped out at the CMA Awards…

#845. AI is turbocharging cyberattacks — can computer scientists catch up?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

David Adam is a journalist based near London and author of The Man Who Couldn’t Stop (2014) and The Genius Within (2018).

Artificial intelligence systems are transforming the way software vulnerabilities are discovered.Credit: Hailshadow/Getty

The disruption of multiple computer systems run by Microsoft, US air traffic control, the bank JPMorgan Chase and even the US National Security Agency has renewed concerns about the resilience of critical digital infrastructure.

At the same time, researchers have reported artificial intelligence -assisted discovery of security flaws in Java and PHP software, while hackers have used AI tools to target supermarket fridges and freezers in Europe.

Although probably unrelated, these incidents highlight a broader transformation in cybersecurity, say researchers. Artificial intelligence is changing how software vulnerabilities are discovered, allowing both attackers and security specialists to examine vast quantities of computer code at unprecedented speed.

“I think vulnerability discovery without AI is basically dead,” says Steven Murdoch, a computer security researcher at University College London. Researchers in the field who don’t use the technology now risk falling behind, he says.

AI can find weaknesses in software much faster than humans can, giving attackers time to exploit vulnerabilities before organizations can fix them. Researchers now want to understand how thoroughly AI can check software for security flaws, and whether it could introduce new weaknesses.

Agentic systems help attackers identify security vulnerabilities more rapidly and systematically. While hackers previously had to spend hours inspecting websites and probing software for weaknesses that offered unauthorized access to networks, AI agents use automated tools that can search millions of lines of computer code.

Google has reported that attackers have already used agentic AI to examine software updates, identify the security problems they address, and then find ways to exploit them.

NEWS: Cyberattacks are hitting research institutions — with devastating effects

NEWS: Cyberattacks are hitting research institutions — with devastating effects

“For me, it's about the scale,” says Daniel Gardham, a cybersecurity researcher at the University of Surrey. AI tends to find the same kinds of weaknesses as human hackers, but it makes it easier for people with limited technical expertise to break into systems.

“They can set an AI agent off and come back in 20 minutes and have dozens of results already,” he says.

Even with AI, most security breaches still involve human failure, he says, such as weak passwords (a common problem with Europe’s supermarket freezers was that passwords were defaults such as ‘admin’ or ‘12345’) or clicking on links from unfamiliar sources. AI-crafted messages can make such phishing messages more convincing and so more likely to succeed. They can draw on publicly available information to personalize fraudulent communications and make them appear authentic

Murdoch says AI is particularly good at discovering familiar kinds of software flaws, even if the most accomplished human researchers remain better at finding entirely new types of weakness. “They don't need to sleep,” he says. “You can happily work a hundred of them in parallel.”

These capabilities of AI helped discover security flaws in Java and PHP software, two programming languages that build cross-platform software and websites. In the Java case, for example, AI identified circumstances that could allow an attacker to corrupt computer memory. But Murdoch says the significance of the issue has been exaggerated.

The Java vulnerability, he says: “Is a real problem, but it’s not one of the top ten vulnerabilities this year or probably even this week.”

Just like hackers, cybersecurity researchers are using AI tools to quickly and efficiently find weaknesses in computer systems. Murdoch says this has become increasingly important to vulnerability researchers, who can now examine much larger quantities of software and work out how to patch up the defences where necessary. Researchers are also developing AI agents that can detect and repair vulnerabilities automatically.

When security researchers uncover a weakness, they typically notify the software developer privately, allowing engineers to prepare a remedy before publishing details of the problem.

AI is set to completely transform cybersecurity — here’s how researchers must prepare

AI is set to completely transform cybersecurity — here’s how researchers must prepare

Murdoch says the use of AI in cyber security has shortened the time window between public disclosure and attempted exploitation – from several weeks, to just a few days.

Rushing an update can bring its own problems. A software patch can interfere with other programs and cause the sort of outage that organisations are trying to avoid.

“The life for the defenders who are trying to fix things has become significantly harder,” Murdoch says.

It’s unlikely that the recent tech outages were connected as large-scale cyber-attack, says Murdoch. The most prominent disruptions, he says, are likely technical malfunctions rather than anything more sinister.

#844. From kit boy to manager at 28 - Dumbarton appoint Fellowes

Martin Fellowes has become the youngest manager in SPFL history, taking on the Dumbarton head coach job at the age of 28.

Leaving his position as assistant manager and head of football operations at Scottish League 2 leaders Stranraer, Fellowes inherits a team six places further down the ladder.

With experience on the Scotland Under-19s coaching team, Fellowes spent almost 10 years with East Kilbride, rising from teenage kit boy to a two-month spell as interim manager in 2023, winning the Lowland League Cup.

With a day job in office furniture sales, he holds a Uefa A licence.

"You have to earn people's respect as a person," Fellowes told BBC Scotland.

"When you are a young guy and you're leading a football club, I don't think you can come in and change everything and lead with an iron fist.

"You have to get people's respect on and off the pitch. I know there will be plenty of criticism and there will be plenty of people sitting here today doubting that I'm capable of doing this job at 28.

"But now really the work for me has started on, by the end of the process, having gained those people onside to say, 'he was more than capable of doing this job and we're delighted to have him here'.

"I can only do that through winning games of football."

Martin Fellowes (right) as a 17-year-old kit man at East Kilbride

Jim Duffy was 29 when he began his long managerial career at Falkirk and Rhys McCabe was player/manager at Airdrieonians at the same age.

Ian Cathro, now leading French club Saint-Etienne, took charge of Hearts when he was just 30.

Fellowes replaces Frank McKeown, who resigned last month, while director of football Danny Lennon had been standing in on an interim basis.

The Sons are two points off the promotion places and visit Spartans on Saturday.

"We're not going to reinvent the wheel," Fellowes added.

"We're not going to do anything that anybody else hasn't been doing.

"But if we can add the 5% to every different department and win games of football, I think over time people will understand that sometimes the age isn't a barrier but it can actually be an advantage."

#843. Hungary eases abortion restrictions in women's rights overhaul

The reforms mark a break the the conservative policies of former PM Viktor Orban. The controversial "heartbeat regulation" is to be scrapped and women are to be better protected against violence.

Hungary on Thursday said it would ease abortion rules and ratify an international treaty on violence against women.

Under the planned changes to the so-called "heartbeat regulation," women will no longer be forced to listen to the vital signs of the fetus before an abortion.

Women will also be able to get emergency contraceptive pills without prescription.

The changes proposed by the new government under Prime Minister Peter Magyar are a significant break with the conservative policies of his predecessor Viktor Orban.

The country also plans to ratify the Istanbul Convention, a treaty aimed at preventing violence against women and domestic violence.

Hungarian law allows for most abortions to be performed up to 12 weeks, and up to 24 weeks in cases of severe developmental abnormalities. Until now, women were required to have a medical provider show them evidence of a definitive sign of fetal life, commonly understood as the so-called "fetal heartbeat," before deciding whether to have an abortion.

The controversial 2022 policy had received widespread criticism from doctors and women’s rights groups as being cruel and humiliating. It will now be scrapped.

The policy had not led to a decline in abortions and according to Magyar, had raised "serious bioethical questions."

The second major change is that emergency contraception will be available without prescription.

Further measures include changing the criminal code aimed at better protecting women, including making the misuse of intimate images a criminal offense and strengthening the treatment of victims of domestic violence during criminal proceedings.

Hungary also plans to ratify an international treaty on the protection of women which most other EU members have long ratified. The Istanbul Convention came into force in 2014 and, among other things, requires rape to be criminalized based on the absence of freely given consent.

"We are making it clear that sexual acts can only ⁠take ​place with the voluntary consent of the other party," ​Magyar said.

The government of his predecessor Orban had opposed the treaty, arguing that it promoted what it described as "gender ideology."

"We are making a clear and accountable commitment to putting an end to the era of inaction," Magyar said in a Facebook video.

Among the EU’s other members, only Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Slovakia have not yet ratified the convention.

The Istanbul Convention is a treaty by the Council of Europe, an international organization that promotes human rights and the rule of law across Europe and includes more countries than the member of the EU.

#842. Veerle Buurman scrambles late WCL winner to push blunt Chelsea past PSG

Chelsea were made to work hard for three Champions League points against a resilient Paris Saint-Germain side but their patience paid off, Veerle Buurman squeezing the ball in at the near post to put them, temporarily at least, at the top of the table in the league phase.

Buurman had stolen the show in Chelsea’s defeat of Manchester City at the weekend, coming on 12 minutes in and nullifying Khadija Shaw’s threat to be named player of the match, and she was the hero under the lights with Chelsea doing everything but score prior to her goal.

“She is a top, young talent and is so mature on and off the pitch,” said Sonia Bompastor. “She is a confident player and a really complete player.”

Bompastor’s side were frustrated by Häcken last week, held to a 0-0 draw by the Swedish side and falling out of the top four automatic qualification places. There was a desire to put things right at AFC Wimbledon’s stadium and they did just that, albeit in not the prettiest of encounters.

“Sometimes in football you need to find a way to win and the result tonight was really important for us,” said Bompastor.

Lauren Hemp and Khadija Shaw both scored off the bench to earn Manchester City a 2-0 Women’s Champions League victory over Häcken in Gothenburg.

The first half ended goalless with City's best chances coming just before the break. Aoba Fujino was put through on goal but she hit her effort straight at Häcken keeper Jennifer Falk, who made saves from Grace Clinton and Rebecca Knaak to keep the hosts on terms at the interval.

Hemp and Shaw were both introduced at half-time by Andrée Jeglertz, and the England winger opened the scoring after 55 minutes. It was a fortuitous breakthrough, with Emma Östlund's clearance ricocheting off Hemp's shin and into the net [pictured]. Mary Fowler appeared to have added a second soon after, but her strike was ruled out for offside against Yui Hasegawa.

Soon after Hemp was denied her second goal when her shot hit the post, she turned creator by passing to an onrushing Shaw, who tucked home for City's second in the 77th minute. The visitors could have had a third, but Falk saved Fowler's stoppage-time penalty after a VAR intervention.

Signe Bruun also made the difference off the bench on Wednesday, scoring two late goals as Real Madrid wore down 10-woman Internazionale to win 3-1. The Danish forward put Madrid ahead five minutes of time before adding a late penalty to secure all three points.

Lineth Beerensteyn got the hosts off the mark in Madrid after 28 minutes, and Inter faced an uphill battle after Karolina Vilhjalmsdottir was sent off three minutes before the break. The visitors got an unexpected equaliser when Michela Cambiaghi headed in from a corner, and held on until Bruun's late double.

City and Real Madrid are both unbeaten after five league phase games, winning two and drawing three matches each as they bid to finish in the top four and avoid the playoffs. Juventus join them on nine points after late goals from Annamaria Serturini and Matilde Pavan earned a 2-0 home win over Leuven.  PA and Guardian sport

PSG had lost 2-1 at home to Bayern Munich after three draws and one win in the competition before their trip to London. Denied a point late on, they remain 10th and dangerously close to slipping out of the playoff places with one game to play.

Chelsea had been thrillingly gutsy and diligent in their 1-0 win over City on Saturday and against PSG they were similarly solid at the back, but they lacked spark in attack. Ellie Carpenter became the focal point of their forward play from the right, with the striker Melvine Malard injured in the game against City.

PSG nullifying the threat of Carpenter blunted Chelsea, and despite their dominance of the ball, amassing 64% possession in the first half, Chelsea struggled to carve a way through the visitors’ backline. They had seven attempts on goal to PSG’s six at the break, despite 33 attacks to 10.

Chelsea have historically performed well against PSG, winning three of their four Champions League meetings prior to this penultimate fixture of their league phase campaign. In the 2018-19 quarter-finals they earned a 2-0 home win and, after a 2-1 away defeat, progressed to the semi-finals; in the 2022-23 season they won both group meetings with an overall score of 4-0.

The visiting team’s first attempt on target arrived after the break, with Merveille Kanjinga forcing a near-post save from Hannah Hampton. While Chelsea still dominated, PSG had more forays forward in the second half.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

Erin Cuthbert, Maika Hamano and Lucy Bronze arrived at the hour mark as the home team sought to deal the killer blow their dominance required. It increasingly felt like it would take something special to break the deadlock, akin to the sublime effort that Sandy Baltimore had delivered against City.

Aggie Beever-Jones was replaced by Sjoeke Nüsken late on and the German instantly made a difference, forcing a sublime save from Katarzyna Kiedrzynek. The breakthrough came from the resulting corner, and it was far less sublime than Saturday’s effort, Buurman somehow squeezing the ball in at the near post after PSG failed to clear Cuthbert’s ball in.

“The main feeling is one of frustration,” said the PSG manager, Paulo César. “We defended well, we just lacked a bit of clarity on the transition and I have mixed feelings. I’m proud of my team but it shows that there are very fine margins that we need to rival a big team like Chelsea.”

Ultimately, the goal was the bit of luck Chelsea needed and they look increasingly formidable.

#841. Netflix, Fox and the $2bn bid for the 2030 World Cup that could reshape live sports

The battle for the US TV rights to the tournament will pit the traditional broadcaster against the ‘whatever-it-takes’ streamer. It could be a tipping point in the industry

The awarding of broadcast rights in the United States for this year’s World Cup was a cut-price deal to avoid legal action from the existing rights holders, Fox Sports. This week’s tender process for the 2030 tournament will be anything but.

Media rights and broadcast experts canvassed by the Guardian in the US and Europe are united in agreement that Fifa will benefit from the most competitive and expensive auction in the competition’s history. It is expected to fetch between $1.5bn (£1.13bn) and $2bn, with some predicting the outcome could be a landmark moment for the sports and entertainment industry.

There also appears to be a clear frontrunner. “I would put money on Netflix to win – they will pay whatever it takes,” one experienced media rights buyer told the Guardian.

Multiple sources have confirmed that Netflix would submit a bid before Thursday’s deadline for first-round offers, along with their fellow streamers Apple TV, Disney, Amazon, YouTube and Dazn, as well as the traditional broadcasting heavyweights, Fox, ESPN, NBC Universal and Skydance, although the last of these may find itself constrained by the budget cuts being made after its $110bn acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery. Netflix has already bought exclusive rights in the US for the 2027 and 2031 Women’s World Cups.

“There’s a huge range of buyers and therefore a broad range of possible outcomes,” one broadcasting veteran says. “All the media companies and streamers will bid. Fox will find it very challenging to retain the rights.”

In a significant change, Fifa is selling the English and Spanish rights together for the first time, a move that indicates it is seeking a single exclusive rights holder, which would suit the streaming companies. With Fox having paid $485m for exclusive English-language rights to the 2026 World Cup, and NBC Universal’s Telemundo paying $600m for the Spanish-language rights, the only certainty is that the 2030 price will be far higher, despite less attractive kick-off times for a US audience as the tournament is in Morocco, Spain and Portugal.

The impact of the time difference is hard to price, but may not prove to be that significant given the seemingly insatiable demand. NBC paid about $1.5bn for exclusive rights for the 2024 Paris Olympics and were rewarded with average daily viewing figures of more than 30 million, albeit with far more variation in programming than a World Cup.

Fifa awarded non-competitive extensions to Fox and Telemundo in 2015 as compensation for moving the 2022 Qatar World Cup to winter, a perspective that was strengthened on the back of this year’s record-breaking tournament. Fox’s live coverage of Spain’s extra-time victory over Argentina in the final was the most-watched soccer telecast in US history, with a peak audience of 51.685 million; five World Cup games brought in average audiences of more than 20 million; and the average viewing figure across all 104 matches was 7.7 million, twice the figure in Qatar four years earlier.

Telemundo’s coverage, available through NBC’s streaming platform Peacock, averaged a total audience of 6 million viewers per game, with Spain v Argentina and Mexico v England attracting peak audiences of more than 23 million, the highest-ever for Spanish-language broadcasts in the US.

The bumper audiences were extremely lucrative for the broadcasters, with figures from the advertising sales analysts Guideline showing that Fox and Telemundo generated a combined $1.19bn in advertising revenue alone during the tournament, almost three times the figure from Qatar four years earlier and more than their original rights investment.

Fox alone brought in $835m from World Cup advertising, with 30-second slots costing between $200,000 and $750,000 according to the Hollywood Reporter, and the six-minute hydration breaks generating between $2m and $9m per game.

Having left a considerable amount of money on the table because of the circumstances of the 2026 process, Fifa is determined to cash in this time around. Holding the auction only four months after the US hosted the World Cup appears a clear attempt to capitalise on the success of the previous tournament, which contributed the vast majority of Fifa’s $4bn media revenues over the four-year cycle to 2026.

The addition of hydration breaks will give bidders such as Fox more revenue to play with, although Fifa will expect the option for extra adverts to drive up the price and take its own cut this time around, having missed out in the summer. The two three-minute breaks in each half were only finalised last year and did not feature in the 2026 tender documents.

“Sports advertising is much more valuable than entertainment programming as it has a broader reach,” says François Godard, an independent media analyst. “And one-off events such as World Cups do not generally do particularly well for subscription services, who want year-round content.

“Fox in particular needs the World Cup and is heavily associated with it. They are the smallest of the legacy broadcasters and are reliant on sport, as well as news. Having said that, the market for sport amongst streamers is far more competitive in the US than in Europe. Netflix, Amazon and YouTube have all bought NFL rights, while Apple is investing heavily in Formula One, so I wouldn’t rule any of them out.”

A new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisis

Adam Kelly, president of the global sports marketing agency IMG, has a seat at the table at many rights negotiations and has long predicted the rise of the streamers, viewing the 2030 World Cup as the potential tipping point when a premium event could be exclusively bought in a major market by a streaming service for the first time. IMG has the rights to sell more than 70 global sports organisations, including the Premier League, World Rugby and Wimbledon.

In addition to the exclusive rights in the US for the 2027 and 2031 Women’s World Cups, Netflix has secured exclusive 2030 World Cup rights in Spain. It must sublicense all of the Spanish national team’s matches, both semi-finals and final and at least one match per day to a domestic free-to-air broadcaster to comply with government regulations.

“These entities are the future of broadcasting, as they are the best companies in the world at turning attention into earnings,” Kelly says of the streamers. “Their model allows them to monetise better than their rivals due to their size, scale and the high consumption levels of their customers.

“Netflix in particular has built a sophisticated and lucrative advertising platform. They have the back-office capability and 2027 would provide a perfect test run. If they’re successful in the tender for the World Cup it shows they are potentially the future of sports broadcasting.”

“As a company, Netflix’s unique offering is exclusivity, so why would they hand that to their rivals?” another broadcast source said. “There are no regulations in the US preventing exclusivity so I would expect Netflix to bid for and retain every game if they win.”

Given recent reports that Netflix is exploring tabling an offer for NBC Universal after withdrawing its $85bn bid for Warner Bros last year, a future partnership with a linear network cannot be ruled out if it is successful. Some sources have even suggested that the tender has been timed deliberately to attract a competitive bid from Netflix, as the streamer is short of sports content to promote during the 2027 Women’s World Cup. Others argue that Fifa would have been better advised waiting to build further on the interest created by that tournament.

The NFL’s decision to pause its media rights process as it seeks an early renegotiation of contracts that are due to run to 2034 is likely to have played a part in the timing, creating a window of opportunity for Fifa to go to market. While a second round of bidding is possible after Thursday’s opening round, the outcome is expected to be known within the next few weeks and could present a bounce for Gianni Infantino as he continues his presidential re-election campaign.

#840. Posh chairman MacAnthony 'fighting for his legacy'

Darragh MacAnthony marked 20 years as Peterborough chairman earlier this year

Darragh MacAnthony says he is "working around the clock" to protect his "legacy" as Peterborough United chairman, with the club facing another fight to retain their League One status.

Posh's hierarchy had targeted promotion in 2026-27, but are 22nd in the third-tier, having finished 18th in the past two seasons.

Peterborough sacked manager Luke Williams after 11 months in charge in September and appointed Robbie Savage, but they are on a run of no win in seven games in all competitions.

Last month, MacAnthony "promised" to sell his 75% stake in the club after 20 years as chairman if they had not reached League One's top 10 by February.

On Tuesday, MacAnthony issued a lengthy statement on the club's website, external in which he said he "would not outstay my welcome at this amazing club".

"If we don't turn things around, I will look to put the club in the hands of someone who can do a better job than me, because that is the right thing to do," the statement added.

"It is not something I want to do or need to do, but if it is right for our club, it will get done. You have my word on that."

MacAnthony sold half his stake to Jason Neale and Stewart Thompson in 2018, through their Canadian business Kelgary Sports and Entertainment, but became sole majority shareholder again five years later after they stood down from the board.

"I am working around the clock to make sure my legacy as owner will not be defined by this season," MacAnthony said.

"I have been in this game long enough to know there will be more downs before the highs return, but I have staked my ownership on the highs returning.

"I have done that because, as always, I am an eternal optimist, and I honestly believe our club, our players and our staff will turn this awful time around for you, our fans."

#839. Strasbourg appoint Swansea boss Matos

Vitor Matos was under contract at Swansea until 2030

Strasbourg have announced the appointment of Swansea City's Vitor Matos as the club's new head coach.

The French top-flight side made the announcement on Wednesday evening, but there has been no confirmation of Matos' departure from the Swans.

Strasbourg are expected to pay Swansea compensation thought to be in the region of Â£5m in order to secure his services.

Matos, 38, spent just under a year at Swansea having left his role at Maritimo to succeed Alan Sheehan as the Championship club's head coach in November 2025.

Four members of Matos' coaching team - Diogo Medeiros, Toze Mendes, Goncalo Ricca and head of goalkeeping Pedro Pereira - are also expected to leave Swansea.

Ex-captain Ashley Williams is set to return to the club to join an interim coaching team also featuring fellow former players Kristian O'Leary and Leon Britton.

O'Leary and Britton are set to be the only remaining members of Matos' Swansea staff.

Alongside Williams, they will lead Swansea while the club searches for Matos' permanent successor.

Their first game will be at home to West Bromwich Albion on Saturday.

Swansea go to Middlesbrough next Tuesday before hosting rivals Cardiff City on Sunday, 29 November.

Matos moves on despite agreeing an extended Swansea contract running until 2030 in July.

Leon Britton (left) and Ashley Williams (right) were Swansea team-mates in League One, the Championship and the Premier League

Swansea were 20th in the second tier when the former Liverpool coach took over, but he leaves a team lying only three points off the top of the table in sixth.

Matos led Swansea to an 11th-placed finish last season, and has raised hopes of a potential promotion push in 2026-27 thanks to an encouraging start to this campaign.

But he told Swansea he wanted to move on after Strasbourg, who have the same ownership group as Premier League side Chelsea, made their move last weekend and he said goodbye to players and staff on Tuesday.

Having finished eighth last season, Strasbourg are 13th in Ligue 1 having won only three of their 10 league games under Hugo Oliveira, who was only appointed in the summer after Gary O'Neil departed to take over at Ipswich Town.

Latest Swansea City news, analysis and fan views

Listen to the latest Swansea City interviews, news and discussion on BBC Sounds

Matos was touted as a contender to take charge at Crystal Palace earlier this season - the Eagles have since appointed Thomas Frank - while he had also been linked with a return to Portugal on the back of his impact at Swansea.

When asked in October about the Palace links, Matos said: "I'm Swansea manager. I love being here, love my players, love the staff, so my focus is always on the next game and what we can do better."

In an interview last week, Swansea chief executive Tom Gorringe acknowledged that Matos' impact will not have gone unnoticed at other clubs.

But Gorringe played down the idea of Matos being lured away, saying: "The reality is there'll always be interest in anyone performing well in any role on and off the pitch.

"That's one of the outcomes of being successful - we're aware of that.

"[But] we're all quite happy. We've all agreed to go on this journey together and we hope that Vitor is here a long time."

#837. Travis Kelce Supports Taylor Swift's CMA Awards Performance From Afar

Travis Kelce proved he is always Taylor Swift's no. 1 fan after she performed at the 2026 CMA Awards on Nov. 18, even though he didn't attend with his wife.

Best believe the singer was bejeweled when she walked in the room to perform her song "I Knew It, I Knew You" at the 2026 CMA Awards. And though Travis Kelce wasn't at Bridgestone Arena to cheer on his wife, he did share his support online.

After all, the Kansas City Chiefs tight end hit the like button on the Nov. 18 Instagram video of her performance—her first at the annual country music awards show since 2013—posted by Swift's official Taylor Nation account.

Swift proved there was magic in the air as she swapped her bold yellow Oscar de la Renta gown for the perfect homage to Toy Story's Jessie: a frock and cowgirl boots. And she didn't shake off her country roots, mashing up her new track with 2007's "Our Song" from her debut album.

While Swift attended the show without her husband—whose team beat the Atlanta Falcons 35-13 on Nov. 15—host Lainey Wilson and longtime friend Brad Paisley teased the newlyweds for hosting their nuptials at the home of the New York Knicks and the New York Rangers in July.

"I'll never forget what my husband said to me when we went looking for a wedding venue," Wilson—who married Devlin "Duck" Hodges in May—said before breaking out into song with Paisley: "'I beg your pardon, but I never promised you Madison Square Garden.'"

The "Patient Zero" singer was hanging tight, honey, as she laughed into pal Brittany Mahomes' shoulder after the joke—a reference to Lynn Anderson's 1999 hit "I Beg Your Pardon (I Never Promised You A Rose Garden)."

Swift mouthed to Wilson and Paisley—both of whom attended her fairy-tale wedding—after the quip, "That was good."

As for why Swift and Kelce decided MSG was the perfect location for their white-veil occasion?

"We wanted to do it somewhere where we could have a very intimate and genuine setting without a lot of distractions," the NFL player explained on his New Heights podcast in September. "We needed it to be a private feel. MSG went above and beyond to give us that.”

But it wasn't just the venue itself that helped sparks fly that evening in July.

"I can't thank everybody enough that showed up, but also that helped put the show on," Kelce continued. "It was so cool to see everyone from my childhood not only mesh with Taylor, but [the people] from her childhood and her family and friends."
