#836. What have the talks with Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi achieved for Ukraine?

The first trilateral talks between Ukraine, the US and Russia in nine months have ended with an agreement on exchanging prisoners. Does this mark a genuine breakthrough and a step toward peace?

The two-day talks between delegations from Ukraine, the US and Russia in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 ended without a ceasefire agreement.

The main outcome was an agreement on a prisoner exchange.

"We have agreed on the largest humanitarian release of prisoners, and tomorrow we will finalize the numbers," Jared Kushner announced after the talks. US envoys Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow on Thursday, where they are due to meet President Vladimir Putin.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had earlier suggested an exchange of "1,000 for 1,000" prisoners, or "1,500 for 1,500." Russia said a large-scale prisoner exchange with Ukraine could take place within the next two to three weeks.

Following the meetings, Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram that the parties had discussed security guarantees and that "the first step should be ending this war and ensuring Ukraine's security." He also stressed that Europe should be involved "at every stage of genuine diplomacy."

Experts interviewed by DW agree that the main outcome of the talks is humanitarian.

"The agreement on a prisoner exchange is already a major step forward," says Artjom Bronzhukov of the Ukrainian think tank Polityka.

Pavlo Lakiychuk of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies Strategy XXI also viewed it as a "very tangible result." He told DW that "getting our people back is already a major success. That is why it is worth continuing."

A real breakthrough, he added, would be the release of civilian detainees from territories occupied since 2014, particularly people from Crimea, who have been held in Russian prisons for years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Davyd Arakhamia, head of the ruling Servant of the People parliamentary faction and Ukraine's representative at the talks in Abu Dhabi, gave a positive assessment of the trilateral talks with the US and Russia, expressing hope that an agreement could be reached by the end of the year.

"I think the Russians came with extremely strict instructions, and it was difficult to ease the tone of the discussion. But the way the US representatives structured the talks with a view to the postwar situation in both countries opened up a dialogue, in my opinion, and allowed us to work together more productively," Arakhamia said at a joint press conference with US and Ukrainian representatives following the talks.

Iuliia Osmolovska of the Kyiv office of the international think tank GLOBSEC cautions against reading too much into the positive assessments of the talks from Washington and Kyiv.

"Diplomats taking part in negotiations will never say that everything went badly and that they have no expectations. Even when no results are achieved, they will still emphasize that the talks were constructive," she said. "For anyone familiar with diplomatic language, these are simply standard phrases."

Osmolovska points to a joint assessment by 71 Ukrainian security and defense experts published by GLOBSEC in the summer. According to the assessment, the chances of a peace agreement or at least a ceasefire being reached this year or next stand at just 19%.

She blames this on the fact that neither side is "ready" for genuine negotiations. Russia, in particular, has yet to accept that its objectives cannot be achieved by military means. "What we are seeing now is more of a farce, an attempt by all sides to put a brave face on things and create the impression that something is moving forward," Osmolovska said.

Artjom Bronzhukov sees the talks as a way for Moscow to buy time.

"The visits by the Russian delegation, particularly under the leadership of Vladimir Medinsky, are nothing more than an attempt to stall and sell empty promises to the US administration in the form of grand agreements, in order to continue receiving so-called gestures of goodwill from Washington, such as the lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel," the political scientist says.

Ahead of the talks, several Western media outlets reported on new US proposals concerning disputed territories. The Economist, for example, reported on a proposal to redraw the administrative boundaries of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. However, a member of the Ukrainian delegation stressed that there had "never been any discussion of concessions on territories occupied by Russia."

Washington made no official comment on the reports.

Kyrylo Budanov, a member of the negotiating delegation and head of the Ukrainian president's office, declined to say whether Russia had used the talks to demand that Ukrainian troops withdraw from the Donbas. Asked by journalists whether Moscow was still insisting that Ukraine pull out of the region, Budanov said the content of the negotiations would remain confidential until an agreement was reached.

"The issues discussed in the talks are matters for negotiation. The only thing that matters is the outcome. Once we achieve it, it will be made public," Budanov said.

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, took a different tone, declaring that "every inch of our land will be returned to Russia one way or another." He was responding to reports in European media that Ukraine was rejecting territorial concessions.

In addition to the Crimean Peninsula, annexed in 2014, Russian President Vladimir Putin claims the four Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson in their entirety as Russian territory, even though Russia does not have full military control over them.

"Putin is not fighting over villages and ruined cowsheds in the Donbas. He is fighting for geopolitical influence and trying to exploit the collapse of the old world order," says Artjom Bronzhukov.

The expert from the Polityka think tank recalls that Ukraine was already asked in early 2026 to withdraw its troops from the part of the Donbas it controls and turn the area into a free economic zone. Such a zone "would very quickly become a Russian-controlled area," he warns.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pavlo Lakiychuk questions the idea of changing administrative boundaries.

"Why would Putin stop there?" asks the expert from the Strategy XXI center. In his view, US negotiators are seeking to extract unilateral concessions from Ukraine "step by step" without demanding anything in return from Russia.

Iuliia Osmolovska describes the proposal as "very original," but says it would pose risks for Ukraine's leadership. Even if the Ukrainian delegation agreed to it, which Osmolovska doubts, the decision would have to be explained to the public, which, she says, is not ready to accept it.

The GLOBSEC expert points out that, following the last harsh winter, marked by shortages of electricity and heating, only 5% of Ukrainians were willing to make concessions to Russia in exchange for an end to attacks on the energy sector.

Following the meeting between Jared Kushner, US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Vladimir Putin in Moscow, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he wants to "coordinate positions with the Americans once again." No further trilateral meetings have been announced so far.

Iuliia Osmolovska believes the parties will sooner or later have to admit that the negotiations have reached a dead end. She expects each side to return to military action.

Pavlo Lakiychuk, by contrast, believes the talks should continue, if only to secure the return of prisoners. He is also convinced that Europeans "will always be there," because the issue is not just the Russian-Ukrainian war but the security of the entire continent.

This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

#835. How Taylor Swift Taught Keltie Knight to Make the Whole Place Shimmer

Ahead of E! News’ Keltie Knight releasing her new self-help book The F--k Them Theory, she detailed how a gig as Taylor Swift’s backup dancer taught her to truly shine in an exclusive interview.

What’s a girl gonna do? Taylor Swift taught Keltie Knight that a diamond’s gotta shine.

Ahead of the release of her new book The F--k Them Theory: Self-Help for People Who Are Done Being the Bigger Person on Nov. 24, the Live from E! host detailed how her past experience as a backup dancer for the “Bejeweled” singer taught her a valuable lesson.

“At the time, I was a blonde,” Knight told E! News in an exclusive interview at a New York launch event for her upcoming book, recalling her 2009 VMAs performance alongside Swift. “Taylor was feeling a way—I don’t know if it was her or her team—but they made me wear a hat because I was blonde and I just had a little blang—a little blonde bang coming out. They were like, ‘No this is her moment.’”

And for the Lady Gang podcast co-host, that moment made her realize that she’s not doing all the extra credit to get graded on a curve.

“Being unapologetically like, ‘I want to be the brightest thing in the room because this is my moment,’” Knight recalled. “I think that is something I’m trying to teach in this book which is like, you’re allowed to shine.”

The 44-year-old emphasized that Swift struck a perfect balance of basking in her moment while also championing those around her.

“You’re allowed to be the star of your own life,” she explained. “If you don’t want any other blondes, if you don’t want bridesmaids, if you don’t want if you want to just own your moment yourself, you can.”

Emmy Award-winning TV personality and New York Times bestselling author Keltie Knight's latest release is half memoir, half self-help book, inspiring readers to transform rejection into power, healing, and reinvention.

In the book, Knight also detailed how Swift was the consummate professional during the 2009 performance, sharing that she not only thanked everyone involved in the project, but also was extra conscious of minor details that helped others do their jobs more effectively.

“I really wanted to tell this story particularly in the book because I saw the Eras Tour documentary and everyone was saying, ‘Oh well, if I had a billion dollars I would treat people this nice and do the handwritten notes,’” the former dancer shared. “And it’s like, no. I was, in 2009, a backup dancer for a girl who had never even won a Moonman yet and she was exactly the same person.”

As Knight put it, “The story is really about showing up and being your best and the way you treat people when you’re nobody is the way you treat people when you’re somebody.”

To read the whole story and more of Knight’s wisdom, pick up your copy of The F--k Them Theory: Self-Help for People Who Are Done Being the Bigger Person on Nov. 24. In the meantime, keep reading for how Swift has been bejeweled for every chapter of her career…

1. While Taylor Swift writes all of her own music, she specifically wrote her entire Speak Now album all by herself. No co-writers, just her. The album was released in Oct. 2010, when Taylor was just 20.

2. She grew up on a Christmas tree farm with her family in Pennsylvania. She references her time there on her holiday song of the same name.

3. She's named after James Taylor. That's right, from one music legend to another.

4. She's a former Abercrombie model. Just like fellow stars Channing Tatum, Jennifer Lawrence, Emma Roberts and Ashton Kutcher, T.Swift modeled for the company in 2003.

5. She gave Eric Church her first gold record. Back in 2006, she joined Rascal Flatts on their tour after Church was fired. "Actually, she called me after I got fired. I read in the paper that we were fired. She called and said 'I want you to know that I love what you do,'" Church previously told the Arizona Daily Star. "I joked with her, 'This is your crowd; they're going to love you. You're going to owe me your first gold record.' I was kidding, but when she got her first gold record she gave me one. It came with a note: 'Thanks for playing too long and too loud on the Flatts tour. I sincerely appreciate it. Taylor.'"

6. She has doubled-jointed elbows. During her 2016 Vogue 73 questions video, Swift was asked if she has any "really cool or bizarre" talents. In response, she said, "OK, I'm well aware that this is not a talent, but this is like the only thing that I can do. I have double-jointed elbows."

7. Her drink of choice? Vodka and Diet Coke, as revealed in that same Vogue video.

8. She turned off her comments on social media to "block some of the noise." In her essay for Elle, entitled "30 Things I Learned Before Turning 30," Swift explained, "social media can be great, but it can also inundate your brain with images of what you aren't, how you're failing, or who is in a cooler locale than you at any given moment. One thing I do to lessen this weird insecurity laser beam is to turn off comments. Yes, I keep comments off on my posts. That way, I'm showing my friends and fans updates on my life, but I'm training my brain to not need the validation of someone telling me that I look [fire emojis]."

9. She was originally going to name her seventh studio album Daylight before landing on Lover. But since the album was the follow-up to reputation, the singer thought the name Daylight would be a little too on the nose. So, when Swift wrote the song "Lover," she decided that would be the name of the album.

10. She's the youngest solo artist to win Album of the Year. T.Swift was just 20 when she won the top honors in 2010 for her beloved album, Fearless.

11. Swift made history at the 2024 Grammys, becoming the first female artist to win Album of the Year four times. (For Fearless, 1989, Folklore and Midnights.)

12. The singer's album, Lover, sold over 1 million pure copies in the United States in its first few months alone, according to Chart Data. This was the first album to reach this milestone in 2019.

13. More historic milestones! At the 2019 American Music Awards, Swift surpassed Michael Jackson's record to become the most awarded artist at the AMAs.

14. As a child, Swift wanted to be a stockbroker, just like her dad! But she went on to find her true calling in music, later moving from Pennsylvania to Tennessee with her family to kick off her career.

15. She learned to play guitar around the age of 12 after learning a few chords from a technician who was fixing her computer. She then went on to write her first song, "Lucky You."

16. She's "obsessed" with Phoebe Waller-Bridge. While talking about her love for Fleabag, Swift told Entertainment Weekly, "She makes you crack up, shocks you, and breaks your heart all in the span of a few minutes in that show." Taylor later performed on the SNL episode which the Amazon Prime star hosted!

17. She wrote her own monologue for her appearance on Saturday Night Live in 2009, which doesn't usually happen with celeb guests. Taylor clearly impressed the team with "Monologue Song (La La La)."

18. She's been BFFs with Selena Gomez since their respective relationships with the Jonas Brothers. (ICYMI, SelGo even supported her best friend in Nov. 2021 when she returned to SNL to perform the 10-minute version of "All Too Well.") Back in 2008, Swift spent time with Joe Jonas, while Gomez dated his younger brother, Nick Jonas. The two quickly became close pals, and have remained tight to this day. Taylor even offered to be the flower girl in Gomez's wedding to fiance Benny Blanco.

19. Remember the "redhead named Abigail" that Swift references in "Fifteen," her beloved song about growing up? Well, she and Swift are still BFFs, too! Abigail Anderson is her name, and the singer was a bridesmaid in her wedding in 2017.

20. She's a godmother, holding that distinction for Jaime King's son Leo Thames and Blake Lively and Ryan Reynolds' daughters James, Inez and Betty.

21. Swift has said that she may never perform her song "Soon You'll Get Better," which is about her mother's cancer battle. During a Q&A session in August 2019, as part of a SiriusXM Town Hall special, she shared, "It was hard to write, it's hard to sing. It's hard to listen to for me, but sometimes music is like that."

22. She doesn't have X, formerly known as Twitter, on her phone. In an interview with Billboard, Swift explained, "Sometimes, when I open Twitter, I get so overwhelmed that I just immediately close it. I haven't had Twitter on my phone in a while because I don't like to have too much news. Like, I follow politics, and that's it. But I don't like to follow who has broken up with who, or who wore an interesting pair of shoes. There's only so much bandwidth my brain can really have."

23. She's never been to therapy. "I talk to my mom a lot, because my mom is the one who's seen everything," Swift told Rolling Stone in September 2019. "God, it takes so long to download somebody on the last 29 years of my life, and my mom has seen it all."

24. According to an interview, her favorite lyrics off of her Lover album are, "Ladies and gentlemen, will you please stand? / With every guitar string scar on my hand/I take this magnetic force of a man to be my lover."

25. Swift is a billionaire! According to an Oct. 2024 report published by Bloomberg, after breaking records in the industry for over a decade, Swift's Eras Tour helped her achieve billionaire status.

26. The 2019 Netflix film, Someone Great, inspired her music, "I cried watching the movie. 28. She's over hiding from cameras: In fact, she's proudly supported husband Travis Kelce at NFL games since 2023. “When you say a relationship is public, that means I’m going to see him do what he loves, we’re showing up for each other, other people are there and we don’t care,” she told Time. “The opposite of that is you have to go to an extreme amount of effort to make sure no one knows that you’re seeing someone. 29. Speaking of Kelce, when Swift and the NFL star announced their engagement on Instagram in August 2025, it made history on the platform, with Billboard—citing date from Meta—reporting that it received over a million reposts.

30. The engagement also helped inspire Cambridge Dictionary’s 2025 word of the year, "Parasocial."

31. Swift made history following the Oct. 2025 release of her album, The Life of a Showgirl, which sold 2.7 million copies in its first day of release, according to the AP.

32. Oh, and the album went on to sell 4 million copies in its first week alone.

33. In The End of an Era, her Disney+ docuseries, Swift said that two factors led to the creation of The Eras Tour: The sale of her masters and the pandemic.

#834. Leicester split with sponsor after porn actress row

BC Game has been the main shirt sponsor of Leicester City for two and a half years

Leicester City have parted ways with their main shirt sponsor after the gambling firm appointed a porn actress as an ambassador.

BC Game - which was named as a sponsor for the League One side at the start of the 2024-25 season - named Eva Elfie as a brand ambassador earlier this month.

The online gambling company posted a video of Elfie and a delivery driver on social media, with the caption: "Welcome to BC Game Eva Elfie! Let the fun begin."

The club, which had faced criticism from fans' group The Foxes Trust, said it had reached a "mutual agreement" to end its partnership with the firm, and supporters who had bought shirts in the past 28 days could exchange them.

Announcing the club's partnership in 2024, Leicester City said BC Game - which is not available to users in the UK - was a "socially responsible platform" and aimed to provide an "enjoyable and safe gaming experience".

When Elfie was confirmed as BC Game's brand ambassador, the firm - in a post on LinkedIn on 3 November - said she had an "established presence in gaming communities".

Chief executive Ali "Ako" Muhanned previously added: "Eva has built an incredible relationship with the gaming and esports community through genuine passion and consistent content creation."

In response, The Foxes Trust said: "Both gambling and pornography can have devastating impacts on people's lives, in particular young people.

"Partnerships like these bring these two worlds to a larger audience and, by association, link them to Leicester City. Is this who we are now?"

On Wednesday the club issued a statement, which said it and the sponsor had "reached a mutual agreement to conclude our commercial partnership with immediate effect".

It also thanked the firm for the "constructive approach taken in reaching this agreement".

The statement confirmed an "enhanced returns policy" in which it would accept BC Game-branded shirts bought since 21 October for exchange or refund, even if they had been worn or personalised.

The company posted a video announcing its partnership with Eva Elfie on social media

The Foxes Trust said it welcomed the decision.

"Since the partnership was announced in 2024, the trust has consistently made clear that BC Game, for numerous reasons, does not reflect the values of our club or its supporters," a spokesperson said.

"That view has been shared by the great majority of fans who responded to our surveys. The recent partnership with an adult content creator only deepened those concerns and the trust felt the need to once again speak out publicly.

"This statement gained strong traction, emphasising the weight of feeling on this matter. Although we believe that the club should never have gone into partnership with BC Game, we nevertheless welcome this decision to part ways."

A spokesperson for BC Game added: "BC Game confirms that its principal partner sponsorship agreement with Leicester City Football Club has ended.

"We thank Leicester City for the partnership and wish the club and its supporters all the best for the future."

#831. Can the EU make it harder to trick consumers online?

The EU wants to curb subscription traps, misleading sales tactics and features that keep people scrolling. What would the proposed Digital Fairness Act change, and does it go far enough?

You sign up for a free trial to watch a series after work. A month later, you've forgotten about it. Then you find a charge for your new 12-month subscription on your bank statement. Sound familiar? You're not alone. Now the EU wants to stop that practice.

Under the European Commission's proposed Digital Fairness Act (DFA), a company would have to remind you before the free trial ends and get your explicit agreement before it can start charging you. The proposed law would also make it easier to cancel a subscription online and require reminders before certain contracts renew automatically.

The Commission presented the proposal on Wednesday. It wants to give consumers more control over how much time and money they spend online.

"We haven't seen that kind of reform in consumer protection in the last 20 years," Agustin Reyna, director general of the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), told DW.

His organization pushed for stronger EU rules against manipulative online practices. He sees the proposal as a good starting point for tackling problems that frustrate consumers every day.

The proposal also includes a ban on manipulative marketing tactics, so-called "dark patterns." A concrete example: You are trying to reserve a hotel room and the website claims that only three are left, a potentially false claim to pressure you into buying.

A concert ticket that gets more expensive while you're waiting in an online queue raises a different problem. The price could still go up in the process, but the seller would have to show the current price while you wait and tell you the maximum you could be asked to pay.

Online games that encourage users to spend their money to advance are also targeted. Children would no longer be able to pay to win or get to the next level of their online game.

Marketing and personalized ads would need to be clearly marked and restricted in the case of children. Consumers should get the option to switch off doomscrolling functions such as the autoplay of videos, showing one clip after the other. With these new rules, the EU wants to make apps and websites less addictive.

For Christoph Busch, an academic with a focus on consumer law and digital services based at Osnabrück University in Germany, the option to opt out doesn't go far enough. He argues that a version in which consumers actively have to choose to opt into those functions would be more effective.

"But then there is always the question of proportionality," Busch said. "And I think here the European legislators are trying to balance different interests."

These competing interests are particularly visible in the gaming industry, where interest groups have warned that the proposed EU restrictions could hurt developers and leave players with fewer options to choose from.

Video Games Europe and the European Games Developer Federation called the proposal "unworkable, unjustified and disproportionate," arguing that a ban on selling children features that help them win or advance is worded so broadly that it "could cover almost any purchase in a game."

For Busch, this argument doesn't hold. "If your business model is based on addictive design features, then maybe your business model has to be reviewed," he said.

Catalina Goanta, an associate professor of private law and technology at Utrecht University, emphasized in an interview with DW that "regulation can very easily slide into overregulation."

Even though she believes that the DFA is a solid and reasonable compromise, she argues that prohibiting dark patterns and doomscrolling altogether would be too prohibitive. Many of the issues consumers currently face could be resolved by enforcing existing regulation more effectively, she said.

She points to the fact that the EU has made a name for itself in the past by adding new rules and regulations that have made it more difficult to access the European market, especially for small online businesses.

"Instead of having 27 different regulations to adhere to, companies will now only get one," Reyna said.

For him, this speaks for simplification, especially when the responsibility for compliance is shared between online influencers and the platforms they publish on.

According to the new legislation, the EU would have the possibility to impose fines of up to six percent of a company's global annual revenue should the company violate the law.

The European Parliament and the Council, which represents member state governments, still have to agree on the text and formally adopt it. All experts agree that in that process, changes are still very likely.

"It will be a difficult trialogue, especially in this climate of simplification and deregulation with a focus on strengthening European competitiveness," said Christoph Busch. In that climate, it is not easy to add consumer rights, he adds.

Agustin Reyna is more optimistic. "The parliament is a divided house, much more than in the past," he says. "But consumer protection is a subject that brings parties together because it brings tangible outcomes to people."

#829. EU leaders tussle over whom to send to Ukraine, Russia peace talks

A seat at the table for Europe now appears likely following comments by a US envoy who just held talks with Putin. But who will take that seat remains unclear.

European leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent them in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the Europeans will be present at the next meetings.

When asked by DW during the European Political Community summit in Dublin why Europe should only get one seat at the table while the US gets two, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas responded with a wry, ironic laugh ― clearly a sign of the frustration felt by European leaders about being sidelined thus far.

The summit of 47 European leaders in Dublin comes in the wake of a diplomatic tour by two Donald Trump administration advisers, the president's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, to talks in Abu Dhabi, followed by a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

The pair then hot-footed their way to Dublin to debrief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelekenskyy.

Zelenskyy and Kushner also said Thursday that Europeans would be at the table for the next talks with Russia on ending the war.

Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war against Ukraine, alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa. As yet, the EU hasn’t been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz insisted Europe will be present.

"At the table must be sitting Ukraine, must be sitting the Europeans, must be sitting the Americans, and naturally Russia," he told reporters in Dublin.

But he, like many other leaders, played down the idea of appointing a special envoy for the talks.

Zelenskyy is insistent on European involvement in the peace talks.

"Not directly yet, and not yet when the Russians are at the table," he told the other leaders during the Dublin meetings. "But Europeans are already involved. And we need to make sure that Europe becomes a regular part of these negotiations."

Europe’s division over exactly who should be present has caused a public battle to erupt. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote an excoriating letter to Costa last week, bemoaning the lack of unity.

"By projecting the image of a Europe that is in disarray, we are merely serving the interests of those who want this war to continue," wrote Meloni.

European leaders had even seemed divided over their level of frustration about the situation.

Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Jansa said in Dublin that it was creating a "bad mood" among leaders, however Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs disputed those comments saying, "I don’t feel that."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The palpable fear among the leaders in Dublin is that the US will accept Russia's demands that Europe changes the way it structures its own security, mainly through the NATO military alliance, in exchange for a seat at the table.

Putin said a commitment that Ukraine will never join NATO and even the potential rolling back of the alliance to remove new joiners Finland and Sweden, could be among his demands.

"What do we hear from them [Europeans]?" asked Putin during the meeting with Kushner and Witkoff in Moscow. "That once a peace agreement is signed, they will immediately deploy troops in Ukraine. This is a legitimate target for us, so the war will resume immediately."

This is exactly the kind of rhetoric the European leaders say they are most wary of, especially those in Russia’s direct neighborhood.

"Right now, we are in the [Russian] trap," said Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal. "If something is a threat to you, will you discuss your defense with the threat [itself]?"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US President Donald Trump said publicly that he was hoping for a "very big, beautiful agreement" that "might involve all of Europe."

Zelensky said he found the US approach "a bit strange."

Many of Europe's leaders speaking in Dublin referenced previous agreements with Russia that they believe Moscow has breached.

They include the 1975 Helsinki Accords, the 1990 Paris Charter, 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act and the one they consider most important: the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, which forbids Russia from using force against Ukraine unless in self-defense.

The rancor over the seat at the peace talks is drawing focus away from arguably the bigger battle in the EU now ― how to fund Ukraine as the war continues.

Back in October, the European Commission identified a €70 billion hole in the EU’s funding it had promised for Ukraine’s economy.

Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico has opposed any further financial and military support for Ukraine.

But Germany's Merz warned he could block the EU's next seven-year budget unless member states agree to contribute to Ukraine's financing.

#824. Magill returns to NI squad for Greece friendlies

Simone Magill's return is a significant boost for Michael McArdle's side

Northern Ireland manager Michael McArdle has made five changes to his squad for the upcoming friendlies against Greece, with the return of experienced striker Simone Magill among the notable returnees.

Magill, who gave birth to her daughter Skye over the summer, returned to training with the Northern Ireland squad last month but did not play in either leg of the World Cup play-off defeat by Portugal.

The 32-year-old Birmingham City forward has not represented Northern Ireland since announcing her pregnancy just over a year ago and will now be hoping to add to her 95 caps and 28 international goals.

Glentoran midfielder Chloe McCarron returns after an injury-hit spell, while Hibernian's Joely Andrews is also back after missing the Portugal games through injury. Both featured for Northern Ireland at the Euros in 2022.

Kerry Beattie completes the trio of returnees in the 24-player squad after impressing in front of goal since joining Portsmouth from Aberdeen during the summer.

'You can be a mum and a footballer - they can co-exist'

Family, football and Dalglish - what drives NI boss McArdle?

There is also a senior recall for defender Ella Haughey. The 22-year-old West Brom player last received a call-up in 2021, when she was named among the substitutes for friendlies against England and Scotland.

Meanwhile, Kess Elmore, Jane McMaster and Lucy-Jayne Grant have retained their places after receiving their first senior call-ups last month.

Injured defender Natalie Johnson misses out, alongside Mia Moore, Naomi McLaughlin, Charlotte Havern and Leyla McFarland.

Both matches will take place at Inver Park in Larne, with the first meeting scheduled for Friday 27 November before the sides face off again on Tuesday 1 December.

Northern Ireland currently sit 52nd in the Fifa world rankings, six places above Greece.

The Birmingham City forward's return has been carefully managed through close collaboration between Northern Ireland and her club, with both parties keen to ensure she is given the time and support needed to make the transition back into competitive football.

Michael McArdle was delighted to welcome his captain back into the fold, revealing that Magill's family were also involved in the previous international camp as she began preparing for life as a mother and professional footballer.

"I'm delighted we've got our captain back," McArdle told BBC Sport NI.

"We've had on the last camp Simone, her husband Mark and Skye as well, just as a transition for us all to get ready for the future for Simone as a mother athlete now.

"That's the exciting piece for her, but great to have her back in a playing capacity now. No pressure or expectation for Simone. It's part of the process collaboratively between us and Birmingham."

Magill also had the opportunity to get back on the training pitch during the previous camp, taking another important step in her gradual return.

McArdle explained that considerable work has been taking place behind the scenes at Birmingham City, with the club's performance staff working closely alongside Northern Ireland's team to manage her progress.

"There's a lot of work going on at the club just now to support Simone's return," he said.

"This opportunity to be in camp and selected again is that opportunity to take that, hopefully playing minutes as well."

Although she has yet to make a public appearance for Birmingham this season, McArdle confirmed that Magill has continued working and gaining minutes behind closed doors.

"We've been very close with Birmingham since pre-season, so Birmingham's performance team and our performance team work together," he added.

For Northern Ireland, however, her return is about more than simply adding another player to the squad. Magill's experience, leadership and influence remain hugely important.

"Her presence, obviously, is our captain and our leader within the playing group, for us as staff as well," McArdle said.

With no expectations placed on her immediate playing involvement, the priority is ensuring Magill's comeback happens at the right pace, while allowing Northern Ireland to benefit from having their captain back among the group.

Goalkeepers: Jackie Burns (Burnley), Lauren Perry (Montrose), Maddy Harvey-Clifford (Cliftonville).

Defenders: Rebecca Holloway and Rebecca McKenna (both Birmingham City), Abi Sweetlove and Jane McMaster (both Linfield), Ellie Mason (Charlton), Fi Morgan (Celtic), Ella Haughey (West Bromwich Albion), Lucy-Jayne Grant (Galway United).

Midfielders: Chloe McCarron and Aimee Kerr (both Glentoran), Joely Andrews (Hibernian), Brenna McPartlan (Burnley), Connie Scofield (Sheffield United), Emily Cassap (Sunderland).

Forwards: Lauren Wade and Keri Halliday (both Hearts), Simone Magill (Birmingham City), Casey Howe (Celtic), Kerry Beattie (Portsmouth), Cora Chambers (Linfield), Kess Elmore (Sparta Prague).

#823. Why Kacey Musgraves, Miranda Lambert Song Cut Out at CMA Awards

During Kacey Musgraves and Miranda Lambert’s performance of “Horses and Divorces” at the CMA Awards 2026, their vocals were partially cut from broadcast. Here’s why.

Kacey Musgraves and Miranda Lambert might like to cuss (and smoke and drink) but the CMA Awards had reign them in.

During the duo’s rendition of their song “Horses and Divorces” at the CMA Awards Nov. 18, many country fans noticed that their performance was partially obstructed from the broadcast—and that’s all due to the language in the song.

While some stars opt to perform a clean version of their songs to follow the Federal Communications Commission guidelines, Musgraves and Lambert performed the original lyrics, which sees Lambert sing, “I’ve done my fair share of s--t talkin,’ too.”

Those present at the ceremony in Bridgestone Arena in Nashville were able to hear Lambert’s entire vocals, but during the ABC broadcast, there was a few seconds of white noise that confused viewers—especially those unfamiliar with the duet.

Luckily, the country singers’ hook, “hell just froze over” is permitted by the FCC and it exemplifies just how momentous the song—which is featured on Musgraves’ album Middle of Nowhere—truly is, considering the stars were previously at odds which each other.

Musgraves admitted during an interview with CBS Mornings earlier this year that it was “common knowledge there was a bit of soft tension” between her and Lambert—and so she decided to bury the hatchet once and for all by featuring the “The House that Built Me” singer on her latest album.

Lambert, for her part, shared she was surprised by Musgraves’ request.

“I hadn’t heard from her in a while,” Lambert—who split from Blake Shelton in 2015—explained in a separate interview during the same CBS Mornings segment. “She texted me and was like, ‘I need to ask you something but I need to ask you on the phone, like I want to talk about this.’”

Musgraves—whose breakup with husband Ruston Kelly occurred five years later in 2020—noted that while she was putting together her album, she saw a video of Lambert riding her horse online and thought, “‘Hey, at least we’ve got two things in common.’”

And so, she thought of the concept for “Horses and Divorces.” When Musgraves pitched the song to Lambert, now married to Brendan McLoughlin, and said “we need to write it,” the 43-year-old said she was immediately game, saying, “Hell yeah we do.”

As she put it, “It was an immediate yes.”

#822. Iranian activist and Nobel Peace Prize winner Narges Mohammadi shares her story in memoir

Written and smuggled out of prison, the 2023 Nobel Prize laureate's memoir reveals the cost of defying Iran's regime and fighting for freedom.

As PEN International marks Imprisoned Writer Day on November 15, a memoir by 2023 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi stands as a powerful act of resistance against authoritarian regimes.

"A Woman Never Stops Fighting — My Struggle for Freedom, Democracy and Human Rights in Iran," was recently published in German and is set to be released in English in September 2027.

The autobiography "portrays how Narges actually became the woman she is today — and it also reveals the price she had to pay to become that woman," Mariam Claren, spokesperson for the Narges Mohammadi Foundation Germany told DW.

Mohammadi wrote the autobiography in prison: "She was constantly writing," says Claren, whose own mother, activist Nahid Taghavi, shared a cell with Mohammadi for two and a half years, in Iran's notorious Evin prison. "Then, in 2020, Narges was forcibly moved to another prison. All her documents were gone. And she had to start all over."

But she managed to rewrite it all, and her texts were smuggled out of prison in fragments by fellow prisoners and visitors who risked their own safety.

In her memoir, Mohammadi recounts pivotal moments in her life, including her childhood and youth, how she started taking action against gender discrimination, political repression, the death penalty and human rights abuses, and the personal and emotional toll of her activism.

The human rights activist has been sentenced to a combined total of more than 44 years in prison and 154 lashes. For more than a decade, she has been separated from her twin children, who are now 19 years old and live in exile in France for their own protection.

Born on April 21, 1972, in Zanjan, Iran, Narges Mohammadi became politically active while studying in physics at Imam Khomeini University of Qazvin in the 1990s.

In "A Woman Never Stops Fighting," she describes how she started mountain climbing as a student, and organized mixed-gender groups dedicated to mountaineering — a controversial initiative at the time. She also helped establish an independent student organization and advocated for political reform. Her activities led to repeated harassment and arrests by authorities.

She began her journalism career in 1996, writing about Iran's student and women's movements. As her public profile grew, she became increasingly involved in Iran's civil society and human rights community.

In 1998, she married political activist Taghi Rahmani. The couple's twins, Ali and Kiana, were born in 2006.

Over the course of her career, Mohammadi worked with some of Iran's most prominent human rights organizations and became a leading figure in the Defenders of Human Rights Centre, founded by 2003 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Shirin Ebadi.

She played a key role in initiatives promoting free elections, peace and the abolition of the death penalty, especially for juvenile offenders. She also helped establish organizations supporting political prisoners and advocating for women's rights.

Her first major prison sentence related to her human rights activities came in 2011. It marked the beginning of a cycle of arrests and prosecutions that would define much of her adult life.

In her memoir, she describes an arrest that took place in front of her young children. At one point during her imprisonment, she lost the right to call them for several months.

She also details the brutal treatment she experienced in prison, with constant interrogations, beatings and denial of medical care.

Another central focus of her activism is denouncing the psychological effects of solitary confinement, which she had previously documented with fellow inmates in her book and documentary project "White Torture."

"When someone is subjected to physical torture, the scars, blood and infections — dreadful as they may be — serve as visible witnesses," she writes in her memoir. But, she adds, "when someone is subjected to psychological torture, no visible traces remain, and the victim cannot justify the trauma — neither to themselves nor to others. In fact, it becomes virtually impossible to even accept that one has been tortured at all, which causes the suffering to continue indefinitely."

"This is also the goal of solitary confinement: to bring the imprisoned person to the very edge of nothingness — to strip them of their identity and of everything that makes them human," she writes.

Through her relentless campaigning against executions and state violence, she helped bring these issues to the forefront of public debate among Iranian activists.

International recognition of her work culminated in October 2023 when she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for "for her fight against the oppression of women in Iran and her fight to promote human rights and freedom for all."

As Mohammadi was unable to attend the ceremony because she remained imprisoned in Tehran's Evin Prison, the award was accepted on her behalf by her teenage twins, who delivered her message to the world.

Following the Nobel Prize, Iranian authorities continued to pursue new legal cases against her, restrict her communications and intensify pressure on her from prison.

She became the target of a systematic smear campaign, including widespread defamation, gender-based harassment and explicit death threats.

"We are firmly convinced that the Islamic Republic of Iran has deployed its cyber army — which is the second-largest, after Russia's — to this end," says Claren of the Narges Mohammadi Foundation. Conspiracy theorists even started claiming she might be working for the regime, she adds: "And what is truly terrible about this is that when a lie is repeated over and over again and spread over the course of years, it eventually leads even ordinary people to start believing it."

In late 2024, following surgery, Mohammadi was granted a temporary medical release. Doctors warned at the time that a return to prison could seriously endanger her health.

Nevertheless, Mohammadi was brutally arrested again in December 2025, while attending a memorial ceremony for Khosrow Alikordi, a lawyer and human rights activist who died in suspicious circumstances.

In prison, she was held in solitary confinement for an extended period and her health continued to deteriorate, Claren reports. But "thanks to a public campaign, she has now been granted what is known as an interruption of detention for medical reasons."

But "that doesn't mean she is free," adds Claren, who notes that she still suffers from serious health problems — as do many Iranians who have been tortured in prison.

In February, an Iranian court ordered additional prison sentences for Mohammadi, along with a travel ban.

Mohammadi lives in constant fear of having to return to prison any day, notes Claren, and "this all comes with the pressure to which Iranian civil society — including, of course, people like Narges — is currently subjected, with questions like: Will Trump launch an attack, yes or no? Will there be another war?"

Despite this uncertainty, Mohammadi continues her activism. Her international profile also helps her supporters keep addressing publicly the issue of human rights in Iran in the public eye, says Claren: "It is incredibly important that, alongside the individual Narges Mohammadi, the focus also remains consistently on the struggle of the people in Iran for freedom, dignity, and fundamental rights — for the right to sing and dance."

#821. Washington Spirit v Kansas City Current: where the NWSL Championship will be won and lost

Croix Bethune, Trinity Rodman and the Rowdy Audi crowd are among the factors that could swing Saturday’s final

This year’s NWSL Championship blends recurring themes with some newness. For the familiar: the Washington Spirit are in the final for the third straight year, hoping the third time’s the charm after back-to-back 1-0 defeats in their past two attempts. Slightly familiar, too, is Kansas City Current playing the championship game at Washington’s Audi Field, where they lost the final to Portland in 2022 and where they will contend again Saturday.

For the novelty? Neither Kansas City nor Washington, despite their modern dominance in the NWSL table, have won the championship since 2021 (when Washington won). With Gotham’s bid for a two-peat stymied by the Current in the semi-final, here are five things that will decide a new winner in 2026.

Washington’s defensive pressure Washington have allowed the second-fewest goals in the NWSL this year. Through the season and into the playoffs, the center-back pairing of the English defender Esme Morgan and Tara Rudd, the Scottish goalkeeper Sandy MacIver (fourth-highest save percentage in NWSL) and the defensive midfielder Andi Sullivan have been tough to break through for even the league’s most elite attackers. Further up the field, the Spirit’s defense begins with an attacking unit fond of forcing mistakes that lead to goals, with the late-season addition of Clara Luvanga (who has seven goal contributions in seven games for the Spirit) a key impact.

Kansas City, who have scored more goals than any other NWSL team this year, will be a challenge. Defending set pieces will be a space to watch, as they provided the only goal Utah scored against the Spirit in the semi-final, and all the goals Kansas City scored against Gotham.

Bethune on a mission against former team This season’s Midfielder of the Year is representing a team in the NWSL Championship for the third straight year (her second with availability to play). But this will be her first not representing the Spirit. After leaving Washington for Missouri in February, Bethune is facing her former team for the chance to win her first championship trophy.

A bit more poetry: Bethune nearly broke the NWSL’s all-time single-season assists record during her 2024 rookie season for the Spirit. (A torn meniscus cut short her streak, but she still was named Rookie of the Year.) She finally broke it this season with Kansas City. Her creative influence in the Current’s midfield has been crucial to unlocking their goal-scoring capabilities. Bethune’s ability to pull apart Washington’s laudable defensive structure could prove crucial in the final.

Kansas City’s attacking depth Temwa Chawinga is a two-time NWSL MVP for a reason, but she wasn’t the sole source of Kansas City’s 54 goals in 30 regular season games. The Current’s past nine goals (across five games including the playoffs) were scored by six different players, with Haley Hopkins (tied with Chawinga for goal contributions in the regular season) notching four of them. Chawinga enters the Championship with only one goal contribution in five games and no goals since 3 October, but she can break through at any moment. If not, the Current’s surrounding cast of contributors – Hopkins, Michelle Cooper, Bethune and Debinha – seems prepared to make the difference.

Rodman is the Spirit’s gamechanger The Spirit also have attacking depth, but Rodman is a gamechanger whose impact is more lopsided. Her 20 goal contributions in the regular season were more than double the goal contributions of any teammate, and that’s without quantifying the space she frees up for fellow goalscorers with her calculated off-the-ball movements.

In the postseason, Rodman has four goal contributions in two games – two goals and two assists. Coming at the end of one of her best club seasons, a big performance in the final will be essential for a Spirit victory. It would also further solidify her as one of the deserved main characters (and highest-paid player) in the NWSL.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

Will Rowdy Audi make a difference? Stadium squabbles were an unexpected storyline of this year’s postseason. Gotham and Washington faced scheduling hurdles that called into question their home-field advantage and/or forced them to play on less-than-ideal pitches for their semi-finals. But this Saturday, the Spirit will still have home-field advantage at Audi Field, where they’ve earned the trust of a robust home crowd. Whether Washington can turn that familiar, friendly space into the perfect scene for actually lifting the trophy in their third straight final would be a poetic end to the postseason’s stadium woes.

#820. Hailey Bieber Reveals Son Jack’s Favorite Food in Sweet New Video

Hailey Bieber shared that her and Justin Bieber’s son Jack Blues, 2, has inherited her love of a tasty treat in a new Rhode behind-the-scenes video.

Hailey Bieber famously created the glazed donut makeup trend—but her son takes the cake with the sweet treat itself.

In fact, the Rhode Beauty founder shared her and Justin Bieber’s 2-year-old son Jack Blues recently woke her up to reveal his preference for the snack.

“The other day, I vaguely woke up when he was talking in the middle of the morning,” Hailey shared while getting her hair styled in a Rhode behind-the-scenes clip posted to the brand’s Instagram Nov. 18. “He’s like, ‘I like donuts! I like them.’”

The 29-year-old’s hair stylist pointed out that Jack has inherited his mom’s love of the pastry.

“That’s your kid,” she joked to Hailey, who agreed with a smile, “Yeah.”

And as the entrepreneur prepares to mark a new milestone when she turns 30 on Nov. 22, she’s looking back at the biggest experience of the previous decade.

“Having a baby, becoming a mom definitely changed me the most in my 20s,” Hailey replied with a smile when asked what part of the decade transformed her the most. “I always knew I wanted to be a mom. I always knew I wanted kids, and it just totally transforms you as a person for the better.”

Though it’s been over two years since she entered that chapter, motherhood continues to bring her teachable moments.

“I ask every parent this,” Hailey shared. “I think that kids are just in a lot of ways born who they are. That's my biggest learning since having a child.”

As she put it, “I know that that's my kid, but I'm also like, ‘How are you, my child?’”

But there’s no doubt that Jack is Justin’s child, too. After all, the tiny tot may already be following in the Grammy winner’s footsteps.

Hailey shared an adorable video on her Instagram Stories Nov. 12, showing Jack playing some notes on a keyboard, writing over the footage, “blues loves the keys.”

And while time will tell if Jack will one day be hitting the stage like his dad, Hailey previously teased that she and Justin plan to add at least one member to their band.

“I definitely want more than one, but I’m taking it one at a time,” she told Interview magazine in April. “Some days I want two. Some days I want five.”

#818. Joint-record six referee errors in last Premier League weekend

The failure to award a penalty to Arsenal would have been more controversial had the Gunners not scored a second-half winner

The Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel has ruled there were six on-field errors in the last round of games - the joint-highest it has recorded in one weekend.

Each week, the five members of the panel assess all the contentious incidents and vote whether both the referee and the video assistant referee (VAR) have got the decisions correct.

You have to go back to the early part of the 2023-24 season to find the last time there were six mistakes logged.

The statistic does not include correct VAR interventions to fix errors, such as the red card shown to Brentford's Igor Thiago.

In the last round of games almost every fixture had a contentious refereeing situation which was hotly debated.

It started on Friday with a potential penalty to Coventry City for a hair pull by Everton's James Tarkowski.

Arsenal were denied a penalty following a VAR review after it was deemed Kai Havertz was offside.

Tottenham lodged a complaint over a challenge by Leeds United's Jayden Bogle, who was not shown a red card.

And Liverpool argued against a late Crystal Palace penalty.

But which decisions did the KMI Panel rule were incorrect? Some of the votes might surprise you.

Such was the controversy across the weekend, it may come as a surprise that the KMI Panel ruled only two were missed VAR interventions. There have been six missed overall, the same number as this stage last season.

Incident 1: Coventry's Caleb Yirenkyi appeared to have his hair pulled inside the area by Everton's James Tarkowski. No penalty was awarded.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 incorrect, for the on-field decision and the VAR.

What the KMI Panel said: "Tarkowski had a hold of Yirenkyi's hair and the panel unanimously felt that VAR should have intervened."

Incident 2: Arsenal's Kai Havertz was pulled down inside the area by Hull City's Nobel Mendy. The VAR, Michael Oliver, sent referee Farai Hallam to the pitchside monitor but it was not given due to an offside offence by the Germany international.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 incorrect, for the on-field decision and the VAR.

What the KMI Panel said: "Although Harvertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence."

Frank Lampard post-match interview - Everton v Coventry

When the KMI Panel sits down to vote there are two separate considerations.

The first is on the decision of the referee, which is a basic judgement in law and the Premier League's expected interpretation.

The second is on the potential VAR intervention. This takes into account what the referee has said, the available replay angles and the high bar for intervention.

Incident 1: Thierno Barry put Everton in front against Coventry in the 61st minute, but there was a VAR check for a potential handball.

KMI Panel vote: 2:3 incorrect on the field, but 5:0 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "On the balance of probability the ball did accidentally strike Barry's hand. However, the readily available footage did not provide conclusive evidence."

Incident 2: Crystal Palace were awarded a penalty against Liverpool three minutes into stoppage time for a foul by Milos Kerkez on Dario Osorio. But was it just a clash of heads?

KMI Panel vote: 0:5 incorrect on the field, but 5:0 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "A penalty was incorrect with the contact being inevitable. However, it was not a clear and obvious error."

Incident 3: Ipswich were awarded a 72nd-minute penalty against Bournemouth for a foul by Lewis Cook on Abdoul Ouattara.

KMI Panel vote: 1:4 incorrect on the field, but 4:1 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "Ouattara made a clear step across Cook who didn't make a challenge and the referee's decision to award a penalty was incorrect. However, it was not a clear and obvious error."

Incident 4: Potential second yellow card for Bournemouth's Marcus Tavernier.

KMI Panel vote: 2:3 incorrect on the field; no VAR intervention possible.

What the KMI Panel said: "There was a clear, deliberate action by Tavernier to delay the restart."

Some of the most high-profile decisions from across the weekend have not yet featured.

That is because they have been voted to be correct on the field and through VAR.

Incident 1: Leeds United's Jayden Bogle caught Tottenham's Mathys Tel on high on his ankle. There was no VAR review for a red card.

KMI Panel vote: 3:2 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "The majority felt Bogle was looking to challenge with his right leg and his left leg came down on the back of Tel's ankle without the speed, force or intensity to be serious foul play. Two panellists felt that the challenge was sufficiently dangerous to merit a red card."

Incident 2: Chelsea's Cole Palmer went down on the edge of the area under a challenge by Sunderland's Luke O'Nien.

KMI Panel vote: 4:1 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "Clear contact made by O'Nien on Palmer which the panel felt should have been penalised with a free-kick on the basis that contact was made outside the area. One panellist felt that the foul contact was inside the area."

Incident 3: Sunderland were awarded a penalty when Levi Colwill was ruled to have tripped Brian Bobbey.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "There was upper body holding from both players as they progressed into the penalty area before a careless trip by the Chelsea defender."

Incident 4: Possible foul by Senne Lammens on Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki before Patrick Dorgu's 96th-minute equaliser.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "Although Lammens turned away from the ball, the contact he made on Suzuki was not impactful."

The KMI Panel was scrapped this summer in the Scottish Premiership because clubs became frustrated with the voting patterns of its members.

But it is more important in the Premier League, with the results creating a merit table which contributes to 50% of referees' salaries in bonus payments.

Many fans will feel there should have been more than two VAR errors logged in the last round of games.

Yet the KMI Panel does not exist to mirror the opinion of supporters.

Crucially, it uses the laws of the game and how the Premier League expects its games to be refereed as the barometer.

Still, six on-field mistakes - plus the Thiago red card - is clearly a high number.

And fans struggle to understand why it seems to be OK to have these on-field errors, and not correct them due to the high bar.

#816. Summer signings join Lionel Messi among MLS’s top earners: Takeaways from the league’s salary release

How much in player salaries did it take to earn a point in the 2026 MLS regular season? The latest batch of salaries lends some insight

Lionel Messi has closer company at the top of MLS’s list of highest-paid players, thanks to another pair of former Barcelona attackers. The Inter Miami captain is still comfortably the league’s top earner, on a guaranteed compensation of $28.3m. Robert Lewandowski (Chicago Fire) and Antoine Griezmann (Orlando City) have entered the list with the second and third highest wages, while Atlanta United’s Breel Embolo, another summer signing, ranks fifth on a guaranteed compensation of $10.8m. Second-year LAFC forward Son Heung-min sits fourth on $11.2m.

Casimiro, who joined Messi in Miami at the end of his contract with Manchester United, is his team’s fourth top-earner with a guaranteed compensation of $3.54m. This comes after Miami announced his signing as a non-designated player to the surprise of some as the Brazilian arrived on a Bosman transfer rather than a loan-with-purchase, as Rodrigo De Paul had last summer, to keep Miami rules compliant. The MLS Players’ Association lists Casimiro on a base salary of $896,004.

All of these earnings figures were revealed as part of the MLS Players’ Association’s twice-a-year data dump, with the latter installment dropping hours before the league’s postseason commenced. While these figures don’t include transfer fees and therefore don’t tell the whole picture of a team’s investment in its roster, it’s a useful bit of insight in regards to how each team is spending on player wages.

Figures are players’ guaranteed compensation inclusive of base salary and all guaranteed bonuses; does not include marketing and other bonuses.

Thirteen of MLS’s 30 clubs have a new highest earner after a busy post-World Cup transfer window. Two – Anders Dreyer (San Diego, $3.6m) and Mateusz Bogusz (Houston, $2.5m) – rose to the top after the departure of a higher-paid teammate. Lozano overtook the injured Riqui Puig after arriving with the LA Galaxy on loan from San Diego. Lewandowski, Griezmann, and Embolo hold similar status, while Charlotte replaced Wilfried Zaha with Allan Saint-Maximin ($7.2m) earning nearly three times as much as the Crystal Palace great.

Other top-earners signed from beyond the league are Brais Méndez (Columbus, $5.2m), André Luiz (Kansas City, $3.3m), and Kai Wagner (Philadelphia, $1.6m). Two strikers who were traded within the league mid-season signed fresh terms that made them their new teams’ highest-paid players: Rafael Navarro (St. Louis, $4.95m) and Dejan Joveljic (Seattle, $3.7m).

The standout failure of the new big earners is Alexis Sánchez. The 37-year-old Chile legend came to North America this summer, joining CF Montréal and making 15 league appearances for the Quebecois club but failing to register a single goal or assist. His $2.97m guaranteed compensation makes up 24.6% of the team’s wage bill.

Griezmann’s arrival means that Messi no longer carries the largest share of any team’s wage bill, as Orlando has dedicated slightly more to the Frenchman (49.5%) than Miami has to the Argentinian (47.7%). Lewandowski narrowly trails by accounting for 47.3% of Chicago’s wage spending. Importantly, Messi’s contract includes add-ons; a portion of Apple TV subscriptions, merchandise sales through Adidas and Fanatics, and an optional ownership stake in Miami when he retires.

Other notable new wages include former Middlesbrough attacking midfielder Morgan Whittaker (Colorado, $2.0m), former Watford and Everton midfielder Abdoulaye Doucouré (Charlotte, $1.0m), former Manchester United left-back Tyrell Malacia (Cincinnati, $1.04m), former NYCFC playmaker Santi Rodríguez (Columbus, $3.9m), South Africa striker Lyle Foster (Houston, $1.8m), former Celtic striker Kyōgo Furuhashi (LA Galaxy, $1.1m), Tunisia winger Elias Saad (Nashville, $1.7m), former Leeds winger Jack Harrison (New England, $3.65m), Côte d’Ivoire winger Bénie Traoré (NYCFC, $2.5m), former Netherlands striker Vincent Janssen (Portland, $1.75m), Tunisia winger Elias Achouri (San Diego, $2.6m), Scotland goalkeeper Angus Gunn (San Jose, $1.6m), and Southampton loanee Damion Downs (St Louis, $1.6m).

While this exercise cannot confidently include every transfer fee paid, the timing of this year’s drop after the regular season’s end allows us to size up how teams spent on wages against the league table.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Does spending more equal success? There’s a degree of correlation there, but it’s not strong.

How valuable is it to get a point in MLS? In 2026’s wage economy, exactly $512,394.

#815. Off Campus Star Reveals He Won't Be Back for Season 2

Riley Davis confirmed that he won't be returning to Off Campus as Allie Hayes' ex Sean McCall. Season two, premiering April 28, will follow Allie (Mika Abdalla) and Dean Di Laurentis (Stephen Kalyn).

Riley Davis is dropping out of Briar University.

After starring as Sean McCall, the on-again-off-again boyfriend of Allie Hayes (Mika Abdalla), in Off Campus, the actor revealed he won't be back on campus for the upcoming second season.

"I'm not gonna be in the next season," Davis told People in an interview published Nov. 19. "There was a plan for some Sean in season two, and we just had a bit of a scheduling thing on my side and a bit on their side."

E! News has reached out to reps for Prime Video for comment and has not yet heard back.

It's a surprising move, given that season two—which is set to premiere on April 28—will focus on hockey player Dean Di Laurentis (Stephen Kalyn) and Allie's game-winning romance.

As Garrett Graham (Belmont Cameli) and Allie's BFF Hannah Wells (Ella Bright) found love in the first season, Allie was focused on making her mark on center stage after breaking up with Sean—who believed her dreams of being an actress were far-fetched—for good.

Although her ex was sure she would eventually come back to him, he did not account for a certain blonde hockey player casually hooking up with Allie. In fact, she actually decided to bed the athlete to avoid slipping back into her relationship with Sean.

Unfortunately for the friends-with-benefits, their fling—which Elle Kennedy's third Off Campus book, The Score, centers on—isn't as chill as either of them expected.

But Davis—who also hit the water as Noah Bainbridge in Netflix's YA series Crew Girl—told the outlet that fans have "so much to look forward to for season two."

Introduced in season one, Allie and Dean's secret relationship will bring even more heat and ice to Briar U in its second installment as they come to terms with their budding feelings. As their love story continues, Sean does make appearances to wreak emotional havoc on Allie.

But Sean isn't the only man to come between their blossoming romance. In fact, Dean punched former friend Hunter Davenport (Charlie Evans) in the season one finale after learning that he and Allie—who did not know the animosity between them until the fight—had a one-night stand.

While Hunter isn't an antagonist in Kennedy's series, showrunner Louisa Levy shared insight into reworking the character for the TV adaptation.

"Some things had to work a little differently because of the timing and the way we platform them," she explained to Variety in May, "but I promise all the fan-favorite things are still intended and planned. There's still a lot of road with those two."

"He also comes from the same world as Dean, which made his arrival feel organic," she explained of Hunter. "We needed to throw a wrench into Dean and Allie's arrangement to elongate their story, and pulling from that universe felt right."

While fans wait for Off Campus season two to skate onto Prime Video, keep reading for more binge-worthy romance TV shows.

Fan of hot hockey players, passionate sex, a slow burn and a rivals-to-lovers trope?

Look no further than the Crave original series—based on Rachel Reid's Gamechangers books—that follows Montreal Voyageurs captain Shane Hollander (Hudson Williams) and Boston Bears captain Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie) through their decade-long romance.

The on-ice rivals spent years in a push-and-pull of clandestine hookups in hotel rooms while soaring to new heights in their hockey careers. But as deeper feelings begin melting any ice in their hearts, they are forced to come to terms with what they really want—and its potential fallout.

But don't worry, show creator Jacob Tierney proved he'll always be Shane and Ilya's biggest cheerleader.

"This is a gay love story set in the world of hockey, so its very existence is an act of rebellion," he told Toronto Life in November 2025. "But the show itself is happily ever after. I didn't want to subvert too many romance tropes—I love these stories. This show is queer joy for adults."

For Belly Conklin (Lola Tung), everything good, everything magical happens between the months of June and August in the Amazon Video series, based on Jenny Han's book series of the same name.

But summer proves to be different when the 15-year-old returns to the beachfront town with brother Steven Conklin (Sean Kaufman) and mom Laurel Park (Jackie Chung) to visit their mom's best friend Susannah Fisher (Rachel Blanchard).

This time, the teen finds herself in a love triangle with brothers Conrad Fisher (Christopher Briney) and Jeramiah Fisher (Gavin Casalegno) amid the throes of adolescence in this emotional coming-of-age series.

When it comes to this sports drama, watching it with clear eyes and full hearts means you'll never lose.

The five-season series, which ran from 2006 to 2011, follows Coach Eric Taylor (Kyle Chandler) as he guides the Dillon Panthers to victory in a football-obsessed town while navigating personal and professional pressures.

At the center of this beloved series—also starring Jesse Plemons, Michael B. Jordan, Minka Kelly, Jurnee Smollett, to name just a few—is the bond between Coach and his wife Tami (Connie Britton), who work as an anchor for the team.

"We really wanted to deal with the authenticity of what it is to try to make a marriage work," Britton told NPR in 2011. "If you're in what we'd consider to be a good marriage, there's going to be a foundation there. There's going to be a foundation that is solid."

"So on top of that foundation," she continued, "you can rock the boat every which way that you want to, and be able to go back to what's at the core of it."

The early-aughts were full of teen dramas where angst, romance and love were at the center. And One Tree Hill didn't wanna be anything other than that.

Set in the fictional town of Tree Hill, N.C., half-brothers Lucas Scott (Chad Michael Murray) and Nathan Scott (James Lafferty) learn to co-exist after the former is recruited to their school's basketball team.

With Lucas considered a social outcast to everyone except best friend Haley James (Bethany Joy Lenz) while being raised solely by his mom Karen Roe (Moira Kelly), the teen is forced to grapple with a new normal.

In his case, that means playing basketball with his brother—who continues to deal with the pressure from their dad Dan Scott (Paul Johansson)—becoming popular after joining the team and navigating a complicated love triangle between best friends Peyton Sawyer (Hilary Burton) and Brooke Davis (Sophia Bush).

Ryan Atwood (Ben McKenzie), an incredibly intelligent teen with problems at home, finds himself living with an affluent family in the cushy town of Newport Beach thanks to his public defender Sandy Cohen (Peter Gallagher).

As he gets closer to his future best friend Seth Cohen (Adam Brody) in the four-season series, Ryan is swept away by the glitz, glamour and drama of Newport Beach, which includes the misunderstood it-girl Marissa Cooper (Mischa Barton) and her fiery best friend Summer Roberts (Rachel Bilson).

A teen love triangle meets the rural town of Silver Falls, Colorado.

Jackie Howard (Nikki Rodriguez) finds herself living with her mom's best friend Katherine Walter (Sarah Rafferty) on a farm after her family died in a car accident.

Now, thousands of miles from her hometown of New York City, Jackie tries to acclimate to a town that has more cattle than people while grieving the loss of her family, all while developing feelings for Katherine's sons Cole Walter (Noah LaLonde) and Alex Walter (Ashby Gentry).

After the popularity of the To All The Boys I Loved Before trilogy, based on Jenny Han's three-book series, fans returned to the Covey household as the youngest sister Kitty (Anna Cartcart) embarks on a journey of self-discovery at South Korea's KISS Academy.

While juggling a new school, Kitty explores her own sexuality and friendships, as well as learns more about her late mom, who also attended the academy as a teen.

The Australian three-season show—a reboot of the 1994 series of the same name—follows Amerie Wadia (Ayesha Madon) as she navigates Hartley High with her new friends Darren Rivers (James Majoos) and Quinni Gallagher-Jones (Chloé Hayden) after an explosive friendship fallout with BFF Harper McLean (Asher Yasbincek).

Once Amerie and Harper's map of all the students' sex lives is discovered, everyone is forced to attend a new sexual education class called Sexual Literacy Tutorial (SLT, though students pronounced it "sluts.")

From threesomes and wild sex to navigating the grief surrounding abortions and sexual assault, Heartbreak High pushes the envelope when it comes to its storyline.

If you are not from down under, a guide to Australian slang will be your best friend while watching this dramedy.

If you're looking for a college-centered series set in the world of fraternities and sororities, consider rushing this ABC Family show. The four-season series follows nerd Rusty Cartwright (Jacob Zachar) at Cyprus-Rhodes University as he explores Greek life at Kappa Tau Gamma, led by his appointed big brother Cappie (Scott Michael Foster).

Meanwhile, his sister Casey Cartwright (Spencer Grammer) is a member of Beta Zeta and Cappie's ex-girlfriend. The series follows six chapters at CRU, where parties, drama and excitement ensue. Oh, and a lot of beer pong.

In this German-language series on Amazon Video, Ruby Bell (Harriet Herbig-Matten) turns the extremely affluent Beaufort family's lives upside down after she sees Lydia (Sonja Weiber) having an affair with their teacher Graham Sutton (Eidin Jalali). Lydia's twin brother James (Damian Hardung), in an attempt to ensure Ruby's silence, tries to bribe her with money and then with his body.

An unimpressed Ruby—a low-income student on scholarship at the tony prep school—declined both of the arrogant lacrosse stars' deals. But while the pair initially despises one another, it doesn't take long before that frustration turns into passion.

All that's left is for Ruby and James to navigate their budding feelings while grappling with the repercussions of their socioeconomic differences. Will love be enough for a happily ever after?

You really shouldn't wanna wait to take the metaphorical trip to Capeside for this six-season series centering Dawson Leery (James Van Der Beek) and his best friends Joey Potter (Katie Holmes) and Pacey Witter (Joshua Jackson).

The show begins with 15-year-old aspiring filmmaker Dawson and his BFF Joey, who is not-so-secretly in love with him, as they navigate adolescence with their friends in the fictional Massachusetts town. Along with exploring topics such as first love, teen pregnancy, racism, drugs and more, the series was a trailblazer in queer media.

The season three finale, which aired in May 2004, featured the first romantic kiss between two gay men Jack Mcphee (Kerr Smith) and Ethan Brody (Adam Kaufman).

"[The scene] gave millions of people a storyline that was reflective of their reality," Kaufman told Us Weekly in May 2020. "I'm so honored to have been a part of that."
